activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: The '10 percent rule', never raising weekly running distance more than 10 percent, is a popular guideline, but studies have not shown it prevents injuries better than other gradual plans.
story:
Mathis spread the notebook on the picnic table so the wind couldn't take it, which it tried to do anyway, flipping pages past the week he had so carefully labelled Week One. The park was loud with Saturday: a man throwing a ball for a dog that had no interest in it, two toddlers negotiating ownership of a slide, and Charles-Etienne arriving at a jog that he clearly wanted Mathis to notice.

"Recovery run," Charles-Etienne announced, though he had run perhaps four hundred metres. "That's the term. My cousin does triathlons."

Mathis wrote it down. Since deciding in June that he would make the cross-country team in the fall, he had filled half the notebook with tables, and the tables had a law at their centre: the 10 percent rule. Never raise your weekly running distance more than 10 percent from one week to the next. He had found it in three places online, which felt like proof. Thirty kilometres this week, thirty-three the next, and so on up the page like a staircase to September.

Sahana arrived with a bag of cherries and no jogging pretensions. She sat down, spat a pit into her palm, and looked at the staircase. "Where'd you get that?"

"It's the 10 percent rule," Mathis said. "You never go up more than 10 percent in a week."

"Who proved it?"

He hadn't expected the question to have teeth. He said something about coaches, about everyone knowing it, and Sahana, who was the kind of person who read footnotes, pulled out her phone and started typing while eating cherries with her other hand. Charles-Etienne lay back on the table and began to prognosticate about the fall season, predicting a top-five finish for himself with the serene confidence of someone who had completed one recovery run.

Last summer Mathis had tried this same thing, and the memory arrived uninvited. He had gone out hard every day in July, thrilled by his own improvement, and by the first week of August his shins had felt like something was tapping them from the inside. He had spent the whole month walking instead, passing the track with his hands in his pockets, telling anyone who asked that he was resting strategically. That had been a summer of doing nothing carefully. This year would be a summer of doing everything carefully, which was why the rule mattered so much. A rule meant it couldn't happen again.

Sahana turned the phone toward him. She had found an actual study, then another, and Mathis read the screen twice because the words refused to arrange themselves into what he'd assumed. The 10 percent rule, it turned out, was a popular guideline, but the studies had not shown it prevented injuries any better than other gradual plans. Runners who climbed the 10 percent staircase got hurt at about the same rate as runners who increased in other careful ways.

"So it's a habit pretending to be a law," Sahana said.

"It's not nothing," Mathis said, hearing himself get defensive. "It's gradual."

"Sure. But there's more than one gradual."

Charles-Etienne sat up, wounded by his own relevance. "So you're a revisionist now? Redoing the whole plan?"

"Maybe the plan was fine and the reason is just wrong," Mathis said, and found he meant it. The staircase still went up gently. It still had rest days, which he had learned the hard way were not optional decoration. It still had warm-ups, which he had once considered a ceremony for other people. What had changed was smaller and stranger: the rule wasn't holding the building up. Gradual was holding it up, and gradual could look like several things.

He thought about asking Ms. Yoon. She ran the loop at the east end of the park most evenings, an unhurried woman in her sixties who had once told him she'd been running since before he was born, and Mathis suspected she had opinions. But he already knew what she'd say, because Sahana had said a version of it, and because his shins had said a version of it a year ago, in their own dialect. What he couldn't settle was what to do about it. Keep the 10 percent staircase because it was tidy and it worked well enough? Or build something looser, weeks that swung a little more, and trust himself to notice trouble early?

He took out a pencil and turned to a fresh page. At the top he wrote "Version Two," then, after a moment, crossed out "Two" and wrote "Two?". Sahana spat another cherry pit into the grass and watched him do it without saying anything, which was the most helpful thing anyone had done all afternoon.

Charles-Etienne leaned over, squinting at the page. "So am I still doing recovery runs?"

"You're doing a warm-up," Mathis said, and demonstrated, walking to the far end of the field with his arms circling like a man preparing to fly and choosing not to.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: Test-driven development, popularized by Kent Beck, follows a 'red, green, refactor' cycle: write a failing test, make it pass, then clean up the code.
story:
The screen door banged twice before Marcus got his laptop through it, once from his elbow and once from the bag of oranges his grandmother had pressed on him at the door. His grandfather's sunroom smelled of newspaper and citronella, and the wicker table wobbled until Marcus folded a coaster under one leg. He was supposed to be on vacation. Instead he had opened an email from Mr. Qureshi three days ago and found a challenge attached: build a BankAccount class in Java, fields private, access only through getter methods, and before that, a test file. The test file was due first.

He had never written a test in his life. He texted Mannat, who was at a coding camp two towns over, and Mannat replied with a screenshot of a whiteboard covered in the words red, green, refactor, arranged like stations on a map.

"What is that, a traffic light?" Marcus typed.

"Sort of," Mannat answered. "Kent Beck, he popularized it. You write a failing test first. Then you make it pass. Then you clean up the code."

Marcus stared at the three words. It felt backwards, like writing the review of a meal before cooking it. He was used to building the class first, running it, squinting at the output, patching whatever cracked. That was how he had written every program since sixth grade, hunched over the machine until it obeyed. The old way had a certain atavistic satisfaction to it, the same pleasure his grandfather took in planing a door until it fit, testing by hand, by feel.

His grandfather came through the kitchen with two glasses of lemonade and set one beside the laptop without comment. He had watched Marcus type all morning from the doorway, the way he watched weather. "When I built the cabinet in the hall," he said finally, "I measured the opening before I cut the wood. Not after."

"That's not the same," Marcus said, and then, because his grandfather kept looking at him, "is it?" He turned back to the screen. He created the test file anyway, hands moving before his opinions caught up. In it he wrote what he wanted the class to do: a new account should report a balance of zero. An account with forty dollars deposited should report forty. He named his getter getBalance and typed a call to it, and when he tried to compile, the whole thing collapsed, because BankAccount did not exist. The error felt almost personal. Red, he thought. So this is the red.

He built the class the way he'd been taught: private double balance, a constructor, a getter that returned the field. He ran the test and it passed, and something in his chest went quiet and settled. Green. He sat with that for a minute. The test had gone first, and it had shaped the class instead of the other way around, the way a frame shapes a wall. He thought about Mannat's camp, about Mr. Qureshi's due dates, about the pragmatics of it, what actually worked when the code got long and other people had to read it. Maybe the old build-it-and-hope method was not a philosophy. Maybe it was just a habit he had never thought to examine.

Erika called at four, from her job at the garden center, bored and loud. "Did you do Qureshi's thing?"

"I did the test first," he said. "Like Mannat's whiteboard."

"You changed your mind," she said. "Last week you said tests were for people who didn't trust themselves."

"I accede," Marcus said. "Formally. In writing if you want it." She laughed at him for a full ten seconds, and he let her, because she was right and it didn't sting the way it would have last week.

He spent the last hour on the third word, refactor, which he now understood was not a punishment but a cleaning. He renamed a variable, removed a line he didn't need, ran the test again to be sure the cleaning had broken nothing. It still passed. The sun had moved across the sunroom floor and was lying against his shoe. His grandfather drifted past, read the green bar on the screen without asking what it meant, and set a second orange beside the laptop.

"Measure twice," his grandfather said, and went back inside.

"Cut once," Marcus said, to the empty doorway, and pressed run again.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Malcolm Gladwell's 2008 book Outliers popularized the '10,000-hour rule', though Ericsson later said the quality of practice matters more than any fixed number of hours.
story:
The guitar had belonged to Christian's uncle, and it still smelled faintly of the attic where it had spent nine years. He sat on the edge of his bed with it balanced awkwardly on his knee, pressing his left fingers onto the frets until the strings printed pale grooves into the pads, then releasing them and pressing again. The G chord kept buzzing. He adjusted his wrist, curled his thumb behind the neck the way the video had shown him, and tried once more. The buzz softened into something almost musical.

Devon let himself in through the kitchen, the way he had since they were nine, and appeared in the doorway with two sodas he had no intention of drinking. "You're doing it," he said, meaning the guitar, meaning the whole project Christian had announced in June and defended all July. Devon dropped onto the desk chair and spun it once. "My mom found my old keyboard in the garage, by the way. I'm thinking of selling it."

"You don't play it."

"Exactly." Devon said it lightly, but he kept turning the ring on his middle finger, a thing he did when something was actually on his mind. "Look, I read this thing. Ten thousand hours. That's what it takes to get good at anything, some guy worked it out. You do the math and it's like eight hours a day for years. You're seventeen. It's pointless to start now."

"Eighteen," Christian said, though he had done the same math at two in the morning, lying awake with a malaise he hadn't been able to name, the sense that every door he hadn't opened at ten was already closing.

"Whatever. Same problem." Devon picked up one of the picks scattered on the desk, flicked it against his knuckle. "I'm just saying, save yourself the trouble. Come to the lake with us Saturday instead."

He left the pick on the desk and went home for dinner, and Christian sat with his phone and typed the number in, half hoping to find the argument that would allay the dread and half hoping to find Devon was right, so he could stop. What he found was that the ten thousand hours came from Malcolm Gladwell's book Outliers, back in 2008, and that the rule had become famous because of it. Then, further down the page, he found something Devon hadn't read. Ericsson, the researcher whose work the book had drawn on, had later said that the quality of practice matters more than any fixed number of hours. Christian read the sentence three times. It didn't promise him anything. It didn't say seventeen, or eighteen, was fine. It said the number wasn't the point, which was a different and stranger comfort.

He thought about Devon's keyboard in the garage, and about how Devon always said he was going to sell things and never sold them. Devon wanted, Christian suspected, to be talked out of wanting anything, because wanting things at their school had a way of getting you laughed at, and it was easier to perform indifference. But Devon had come over every day since June, and he had lingered in the doorway watching Christian's fingers, and the keyboard had surfaced in conversation three times this week without ever going anywhere near a listing.

The next evening Devon came by again, and Christian was playing, badly, the first eight bars of a song Sahana had put on a playlist for him. "Still at it," Devon said from the doorway, not quite a question.

"You know the ten thousand hours thing?" Christian kept his eyes on his fingers. "That's from Malcolm Gladwell's book Outliers, 2008. But Ericsson said the quality of practice matters more than any fixed number of hours." He let the chord ring out, imperfect, sustaining.

"So you'll be a bad guitarist efficiently."

"Probably." Christian laughed, and Devon laughed too, and neither of them pretended the problem was solved. There was something tautological about the way they always ended up here, Devon warning him off effort, Christian defending it, both of them circling the same unspoken question about what was worth wanting.

"Saturday," Devon said at the door. "The lake. You're coming." Then he paused, hand on the frame. "And don't let my mom sell the keyboard or whatever. I might mess around on it." He was down the stairs before Christian could answer, and the screen door clapped shut behind him, twice, the way it always did.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Reporters Without Borders' World Press Freedom Index, published since 2002, scores 180 countries and counts concentration of media ownership as one pressure on press freedom.
story:
The television over the dinner table was tuned to the channel his father always watched, the one with the ticker and the slogan about speaking plainly. Connor had never thought about who spoke, exactly, until Janice's message that afternoon: "check where we rank, RSF index, you'll die." He had not died. He had gone down a rabbit hole in the library instead of studying for his econ final, and now he was pushing rice around his plate while a man on the screen explained that the whole story about the mill was being overblown.

"You're quiet," his mother said. She said it the way she said most things, as an observation that expected an answer.

"Janice sent me this thing. Reporters Without Borders. They publish a World Press Freedom Index, they've done it since 2002, and they score a hundred and eighty countries on it." He kept his fork moving. "We're not first."

His father snorted without looking away from the screen. "An index. Very scientific. Who funds them, the French?"

"Who funds the channel?" Connor said it before he could metabolize it into something softer, and the table went quiet in that particular way, where the quiet itself was the reply.

The story he'd been reading all afternoon was simple enough. A paper in the city, the one that had broken the mill story, the one that had made the channel's parent company look bad for two straight weeks, had been bought. Not cancelled, just bought, and after that the mill story had migrated to page eleven, then to nowhere. The index page Janice had sent listed the pressures it counted, and concentration of media ownership was one of them, sitting there in the list like it was ordinary, like it was a weather condition. Connor had initially assumed the index meant government censorship only, and had typed a smug correction to Janice, and she had sent back a screenshot with the ownership line highlighted and the word "skill issue." He had laughed alone in the library carrel, quietly, arboreal light falling through the tall windows onto his shame.

"The mill thing," he said now. "Caiden's uncle works there. The paper that covered it got bought by the same company that owns that." He nodded at the screen. His father's jaw moved, chewing, considering.

"Companies buy companies," his father said. "That's not a conspiracy, that's Tuesday."

"I didn't say conspiracy." And he hadn't, he realized; what he'd assembled was duller than a conspiracy, which was somehow worse. A subpoena had come out of the mill story, real journalists had asked real questions under oath, and none of that required anyone in a smoke-filled room. It only required that nobody who could green-light the follow-up wanted one. He believed, on balance, that the coverage had changed because of the purchase, and he was honest enough with himself to know the balance was thin, that a story could also just lose steam, that he couldn't see inside the editors' meeting from his library carrel.

"Mr. Mori was talking about this," his mother offered, passing the beans. "At the shop. He said his brother back home reads four papers to get one true one."

"Efficient," his father said, and there was a small crack in it, a smile he aimed at his plate.

They ate. On the screen the man was now very excited about a celebrity divorce. The ticker promised the mill story after the break, and Connor waited through the divorce, through weather, through an advertisement for a bank whose name he recognized from the index of the mill's creditors, which he had not gone looking for and had found anyway, because the index was a doorway and doorways led to doorways.

His phone buzzed against his thigh. Janice: "did you tell your dad or did you wimp out." He typed "told him" and then, after a pause, deleted it, because what he had done was say a sentence and watch it land nowhere, which was not the same as telling anyone anything.

The mill segment, when it finally came, ran forty seconds. The anchor used the phrase "so-called contamination" and turned, seamlessly, to the bank's sponsorship of the town's summer festival. His father watched it with his fork down, and afterward he did not say the index was French, and he did not say it was Tuesday. He picked up the remote, and Connor waited for the channel to change, and instead his father turned the television off entirely, sat back, and said, "Your mother made a pie."

"Since when do we have pie on a Wednesday?"

"Since the news got boring," his father said, and got up to find a knife.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Claude Monet painted more than thirty views of the facade of Rouen Cathedral in 1892 and 1893, showing it under different light at different times of day and year.
story:
The assignment sheet said ten works, one theme, one artist's statement, due before winter break, and Payton had taped it above her desk at home only to read it forty times without deciding anything. On Monday she carried the problem to the art room, where Ms. Dang was scraping dried acrylic off a table with a putty knife and Peter was laying out his photographs in a long row like evidence at a trial.

"Look," Peter said. "Montane meadows. I hiked up Saturday and shot the same meadow six times, morning to dusk. That's my theme. Light." He said it with the confidence of someone who had already filled out the paperwork of his own genius.

Payton looked at his row. The meadow was green, then gold, then blue-gray, then a bruised purple under clouds. It was genuinely good, and something in her tightened with envy, then loosened into a question she couldn't quite hold. "Is six pictures of the same meadow really variety, though? Or is it one picture six times?"

Peter winced. Ms. Dang paused her scraping. Neither of them answered, which meant Payton would have to, and by Friday, in the library during study hall, she was still circling it. She'd drawn the oak outside the cafeteria window twice, once at dawn, before first period, when the light came flat and gray through the glass, and once at dusk, when the branches burned orange. Two drawings. Eight to go, and a widening suspicion that she was making the same artwork over and over with different crayons.

Zavier slid into the seat across from her with his chromebook and a bag of pretzels he shared without being asked, tipping half onto her notebook, which was the kind of thing he did. "What's the face for," he said.

"The face is for this." She turned the two oak drawings toward him. "Same tree, different times of day, and I don't know if it counts as a portfolio or as cheating."

Zavier chewed. Then he turned his chromebook around, because Zavier's answer to every problem was a search bar. He typed something, scrolled, and stopped. "Okay, wait. Claude Monet. In 1892 and 1893, he painted more than thirty views of the facade of Rouen Cathedral."

"Thirty," Payton said.

"Under different light, at different times of day and year. Different times of year, too. Same facade." He spun the screen again and there they were, cathedral after cathedral, the stone pale blue in one, salmon in another, heavy and shadowed in a third, the whole building seeming to change its mind about what it was made of.

Payton looked at the little grid of paintings for a long time. More than thirty, over two years, one building. It wasn't cheating, what Monet had done. It was the opposite of cheating, and yet it also wasn't variety, exactly, not the way Peter meant it, a tour of different meadows. It was something stranger: one subject held still while everything around it moved. She thought about telling Peter, then worried that telling Peter would sound like a correction, and Peter's row of meadows was already taped to the wall of the art room, and she didn't want to be the person who unstuck it.

She went back to the oak anyway, the next morning, before anyone else was at school, and stood at the cafeteria window with her sketchbook while a janitor ran the floor buffer somewhere out of sight, its drone coming and going like weather. The dawn light was the flat gray she'd drawn before, but she noticed now the way it flattened, how it took away the tree's roundness, and she thought she finally understood her own project, or half of it: the tree wasn't the subject. The light was the subject, and the tree was only where the light happened to land. That felt true. She could also admit, standing there, that she wasn't sure it was enough, that a portfolio underpinned by one idea might stand or fall on whether the idea was deep or just narrow, and no one could tell her which, and Ms. Dang wouldn't, having said only, on the first day, "You'll be remunerated in grades, not cash, so paint for yourself first," which had made Peter laugh and had made Payton feel both comforted and slightly cheated, since money at least was honest.

At lunch she found Peter at the cafeteria table and put her two oak drawings down beside his pretzels. "I found out something about your meadows," she said. "Monet. He painted the facade of Rouen Cathedral more than thirty times, in 1892 and 1893, different light, different times of day, different times of year. So your six might be the most old-master thing anyone in this class is doing."

Peter looked at the drawings, then at her, and pushed the pretzel bag toward her without a word, which from Peter was a speech. Zavier, three seats down, raised his milk carton in a silent toast. After school Payton stood at the window again with a fresh page, waiting for the four o'clock light to arrive and show her what the oak would decide to be next.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: A useful way to predict temperature effects is to treat heat as a product of an exothermic reaction and as a reactant of an endothermic one.
story:
Alexis had failed the equilibrium quiz on Tuesday, and on Saturday her mother had dropped her at the science museum with Troy and Vienna anyway, so she carried the failed quiz folded into her back pocket like a warrant for her arrest. The three of them came to the museum a few times a year, mostly for the darkened hall of illusions, but today the map directed them past a new exhibit case and Alexis stopped so abruptly that Troy walked into her shoulder.

Inside the case, a sealed tube sat above two small panels, one warm and one cool, and its contents shifted colour depending on where the tube rested. A placard said only that the tube held a reaction at equilibrium and invited visitors to predict what a change in temperature would do. Beneath the case was a shelf of dry-erase sleeves with the equation printed inside and a blank space beside it, and a prompt: what does temperature change?

"Write the reaction backwards and forwards until it apologizes," Troy said, which was his way of maligning the whole unit. Chemistry had never apologized to anyone; it just kept its accounts.

Vienna picked up a sleeve and wrote the equation from memory, both arrows, then held the marker out to Alexis like a dare. Alexis took it. She remembered Mr. Sow's voice at the whiteboard the day before the quiz, the way he had drawn the double arrow and said only, "A system at equilibrium responds to a disturbance," and then assigned problems about pressure and concentration, everything except temperature, as if temperature were a topic he would get to and then never did. On the quiz there had been a temperature question. She had guessed. The guess had been wrong in a direction she could not afterward reconstruct, which was worse than being wrong in a direction she understood.

She wrote the equation in the sleeve. Then, slowly, on the right side of the arrow, she wrote the word heat. It looked absurd, a word among symbols, like claiming sentience for an algebra problem. But she had spent Thursday night at her grandmother's kitchen table with the textbook and a cooling mug of tea, and at some point she had written heat into the equation the same way, and the problem had finally opened for her, the way a locked door opens not by force but by finding out it was never locked.

"Heat as a product," she said aloud. "If the reaction is exothermic, heat is a product. If it's endothermic, heat is a reactant." Vienna looked at her, and Alexis realized she had said it as fact without being certain it was fact. "I think. That's how I made the quiz question work, after. Heat on the product side, and then temperature change is just adding or removing a product, which I already knew how to handle."

Troy leaned over the sleeve. "So heating it is like adding product."

"Which pushes it the other way," Vienna said, finishing, and Alexis nodded, though a small cold doubt sat under the nod. She had worked this out alone at a kitchen table with no one to check it, and the museum tube was right there, obdurate, waiting to contradict her. She slid the sleeve aside and lifted the tube from the cool panel with the tongs provided, set it on the warm one, and the three of them watched the colour begin its slow shift. It moved in the direction Alexis's written equation predicted. She watched until the change was complete, wanting the tube to be decisive, and it was, and still she kept the quiz folded in her pocket, because a single tube agreeing with her was not the same as being right, and because she did not yet know whether Mr. Sow would look at her written heat and see insight or see a student inventing physics in the margins.

"Show him Monday," Vienna said. "Make him tell you it's real."

Alexis wiped the sleeve clean, then wrote the equation again, both arrows, heat in its place, and slid the marker back to Troy. "You try the cold panel."

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: An ad hominem argument attacks the person making a claim instead of the claim itself, and it is treated as a fallacy in formal debate.
story:
Luke had been studying Portuguese for exactly eleven weeks, which he preferred to describe as "since spring," and the festival committee had somehow interpreted this as fluency. His mother had volunteered him before asking. The debate exhibition at the Harvest Cultural Festival needed a second-team speaker, the organizer said, and any boy who could conjugate estar was apparently qualified to argue municipal policy for five minutes in front of a folding table of judges.

The motion was that the city should stop subsidizing the festival and instead require each vendor to indemnify it against any injury claims, since the parks department was flirting with insolvency and could not keep absorbing the cost of lawsuits. Luke had read the packet twice on the bus. He understood perhaps sixty percent of it, and the forty percent he didn't understand kept folding itself into the sixty percent like wet paper.

"You'll be fine," said Ryden, who was on the other team and had been studying since he was nine, which he mentioned the way other people mentioned the weather. Kennedy handed Luke a stack of index cards she'd written out phonetically. Half of them were encouraging insults in Portuguese she refused to translate.

The tent smelled of fried dough and sunscreen. His embryonic Portuguese sat in his mouth like a stone. He opened with the prepared line about public money, delivered it at the speed of a man reading a ransom note, and then Ryden stood to rebut.

Ryden said something fast and fluid, and the small crowd laughed. Luke caught the word for "accent" and then a phrase that had to mean something like "tourist." He caught his own name. Whatever the actual sentence was, its subject was plainly Luke, and plainly not the subsidies.

Mr. Reddy, the chemistry teacher who had agreed to judge in exchange for a free churro, leaned toward the scorecard. He hadn't looked up all afternoon. Now he did.

Luke's face went hot, and the prepared rebuttal about vendor liability evaporated entirely. He stood there with his index cards and thought, with unusual clarity for someone whose knees were shaking, that Ryden hadn't answered a single point about who pays when the money runs out. He'd just made it about Luke.

"Ad hominem," Luke said, first in English, then again in his careful, freighted Portuguese, because he'd learned the phrase that week and it was one of the maybe two hundred words he actually owned. He turned to Mr. Reddy and the other judges. "In formal debate, that's a fallacy. He attacks the person. Not the argument." Then, because the cards were useless now, he pointed at the parks budget and said, slowly, that the question was not how Luke talked but whether the city could pay, and if it couldn't, the vendors couldn't either, and the festival would simply end, which Ryden had not addressed and presumably would not, since he had spent his three minutes on Luke's vowels.

The crowd didn't laugh this time. Kennedy said something in Portuguese that sounded like an encouraging insult. Ryden's rebuttal, when it came, was quieter and about the actual motion, and it was good, and Luke understood maybe half of it and could not have answered any of that half, so he sat down.

The judges conferred for a long minute. Mr. Reddy wrote something, crossed it out, wrote something else. When they announced the result, Ryden's team won on argument, two judges to one, but the third judge, a woman with a lanyard and a whistle, said in Portuguese that points had been deducted for the personal attack, which was not permitted in formal rounds. Ryden shrugged in a way that conceded nothing and everything.

Afterward, outside the tent, Kennedy bought Luke a fried dough thing and told him his pronunciation of "fallacy" had been, in her opinion, fallacious. Ryden waited until she went for napkins.

"You knew the word," he said, in English, almost approving. "Eleven weeks and you knew the word."

"It's one of two hundred," Luke said. "You should hear me say 'grapefruit.'"

Ryden laughed, and it was not a mean laugh, though Luke filed it away to be sure. They stood by the fence where the vendors were packing up their tables, arguing quietly about whether any of them could actually afford the insurance, and the loudspeaker called for someone's lost jacket.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: A Hanukkah menorah has nine branches: eight for the nights of the holiday and one for the shamash, the helper candle used to light the others, one more each night.
story:
The park had been strung with lights between the lampposts, and the folding tables near the pavilion held platters of latkes going soft under foil. Ashton's mother had volunteered him for the children's craft table before he could object, which was a mannerism of hers, deciding aloud for him and then smiling as though he had agreed. So he sat behind a card table of construction paper dreidels while his little cousins ran between the benches, and Vanessa from his physics class stood at the edge of the crowd holding a paper plate she wasn't eating from.

"You're Jewish," she said when she drifted over. It came out as a question even though it wasn't one.

"Half," he said. "My mom converted before I was born, so I've never known anything else, and my dad's parents still send Christmas cards in December that say Happy Hanukkah, as if those are interchangeable." He softened it with a shrug because Vanessa looked like she was cataloguing something.

The rabbi's assistant had set up the big menorah on the pavilion stage, the public one the parks department allowed now after some meeting Ashton's mother had attended and spoken at. Someone had decided that the town's holiday display ought to enfranchise everyone, so there was a crèche by the fountain and a menorah here and a banner that read, in slightly crooked letters, Festival of Lights and Community. Tonight was the fourth night, and the assistant had handed Ashton the box of candles and a lighter because his mother had said, loudly, that Ashton knew the blessings.

He did know the blessings. What he did not know, standing in front of sixty people who had stopped talking, was how many candles to put in.

He had counted the box twice in his pocket and come up with different numbers, and the menorah's arms curved away from him so the far branches were hard to see. Five? Three? He remembered his grandfather lifting him to the sink-side menorah when he was small, the same ritual each year, but memory gave him warmth and no arithmetic. Mikaela, who was running the sound board for the fifth graders' choir, leaned toward him and stage-whispered, "You're going facetious on us or you're counting?"

"Counting," he said. "Badly."

Ms. Cho, who taught down the hall from his mother at the middle school and came to this every year with her own thermos, was near the front. She caught his eye the way teachers do, the look that says solve it, don't freeze. And then he saw it, the candle set slightly apart, raised or offset from the row, the one he'd been ignoring because it didn't match the pattern of the others. He hadn't placed it; the assistant had, or his mother had, or it was just always there.

"That one's the shamash," he said to Vanessa, quiet, the word surfacing whole from some year of Hebrew school. "The helper candle. You light the others with it. Eight branches for the eight nights, and the ninth is that one."

"So it's not one of them?"

"It's the one that does the lighting." He said it and found he liked saying it, the way a fact you'd forgotten you knew sits in the mouth. He set four candles into the arms for the nights already passed, plus one for tonight, and lifted the shamash out. The crowd's murmur had returned behind him, kids jostling, someone's phone flash going off near the latke table. He sang the first blessing with his mother's voice joining from the third row, and he lit them right to left, or left to right, and only afterward, walking back to the craft table with the lighter still in his pocket, did it occur to him that he might have started at the wrong end. Nobody had corrected him. Maybe you couldn't tell, four candles into eight, which end was which; maybe the whole town was watching a mistake and calling it tradition.

Vanessa had stayed near the stage, plate finally abandoned on a bench. "So which of your halves was that," she asked, and it wasn't cruel, it was the kind of question people ask when they genuinely want the inventory.

"The one that knows the words," he said, and then, because that wasn't true either, "Both. My dad stands in the back and mouth-hums." He nodded toward the fence where his father was, in fact, mouth-humming, hands in his coat pockets. Ashton picked up a paper dreidel and a stub of gold crayon and held them out to her. She took the crayon and turned it once in the cold air, and out by the menorah the fifth graders began to sing.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: Psychologist John Gottman distinguishes a complaint, which addresses a specific behavior, from criticism, which attacks the person's character.
story:
The gym smelled like rubber and floor wax, and Jeremy stood under the far basket with a clipboard he did not know how to hold. Mr. Somsak had named him captain that morning, which everyone knew meant one thing: captains gave the feedback now, not the coaches. Practice had ended, but Isabel was still shooting free throws, alone, her ponytail going gray with sweat, and everyone else had left except Noa, who was pretending to retie his shoes long enough to see what Jeremy would do.

The problem was simple and awful. Isabel had missed practice twice that week, and both times the offense had collapsed into a scrimmage they lost by twenty. Mr. Somsak had said nothing about it, which was his way of saying everything. Jeremy had a speech drafted in his head, and it began, the way his father's speeches began, with you always. You always disappear when it matters. He'd rehearsed it in the shower and it had sounded strong there, and terrible everywhere else.

"Say it to me first," Noa said, bouncing a ball off his own forehead. "The speech. Go."

Jeremy gave him the shower version. Noa stopped bouncing the ball.

"That's the thing," Noa said, pulling out his phone. "My sister makes me listen to this psychology podcast on drives home. The Gottman guy. He says a complaint addresses a specific behavior, but criticism attacks the person's character. Complaint is you missed practice twice. Criticism is you're unreliable." He turned the screen toward Jeremy like it was evidence at trial. "You just went full criticism. On me. And I didn't even do anything."

"That's semantics," Jeremy said.

"It's the whole game, actually."

Jeremy argued for a minute, because the big version felt truer, felt like it carried the weight of the twenty-point loss. Then he thought about how the shower speech had made even him flinch, and how his father's you always speeches had never once made him change anything, only made him want to slam doors. Maybe the small version, the boring one, the one that said you missed practice twice and we fell apart without you, was not weaker. Maybe it was just harder, because it left nowhere to hide. He turned the clip of the scrimmage over in his mind and found, underneath his anger, a compliment wearing a disguise: they had fallen apart without her.

He walked to the free throw line. "You missed practice twice this week," he said, and his voice came out flatter than he wanted, so he pushed on. "Both times we had no one at the top of the key, and Coach had me running your spot, and I'm slow, and it was bad. Also we need you. That's it. That's the whole thing."

Isabel held the ball at her hip for a long moment. "My grandmother's at St. Anne's," she said. "Renal stuff. Tuesdays and Thursdays I sit with her because my mom works nights." She shot the free throw and made it, because of course she did. "I was going to tell Coach Monday."

Jeremy felt the clip in his hand become very heavy. The specific complaint had landed, exactly as advertised, but it had also exposed how little he had known, and he stood there recalibrating. "Okay," he said. "Then, can I say the actual complaint? Two Tuesdays in a row we had no plan at the key. Not you, the plan. If you know Tuesdays are hospital days, someone should be running your spot all season, not me, because I'm genuinely terrible at it. Noa's faster."

"I'm effusive with gratitude," Noa called from the bench, though what he mostly was, was smug.

Isabel laughed, a short exhausted sound that seemed to enervate all the drama out of the gym, and Jeremy understood something he could not yet put in a sentence: that he would have to keep choosing between the satisfying speech and the useful one, and would not always know which was which, and that this was apparently going to be the rest of his life. Mr. Somsak appeared in the doorway with the ball rack, saying nothing, watching.

"Also," Jeremy added, because it suddenly seemed urgent, "I hoard the ball. Three times in the scrimmage I shot when you were open under the basket. Somebody should have said it to me weeks ago." He handed her the clipboard, useless thing, and pointed at the empty key. "Show me the read. I'll pass this time, I promise, and I only always break promises on Tuesdays."

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: The Truman Doctrine, announced in March 1947, pledged US support for countries resisting communist pressure, starting with aid to Greece and Turkey.
story:
The war memorial sat at the edge of the park where the town stopped pretending to be anything but cornfields, a granite soldier staring west while Eric spread his timeline across the base with clothespins from his backpack. He had meant to build it at his grandfather's house, but his grandfather's table was covered with tax papers and his patience was thinner than the paper, so here he was, wind snapping the index cards, Maggie holding the far end down with a thermos.

"Move over," Alexane said, arriving with her own stack of cards. She had picked the opposing historian for the same assignment, and Mr. Holloway had suggested, with a smile Eric distrusted, that they compare notes before the debate on Thursday.

Eric pinned his first card. The Long Telegram, February 1946. Kennan's warning from Moscow, the seed of containment. His historian, the mercurial one whose lectures swung from irony to fury in a single paragraph, argued the Cold War began there, in a cable no one read aloud, the moment the United States understood the Soviet Union as an adversary rather than an ally.

"So your side says it starts with a mood," Alexane said. "A diplomat's bad night."

"My side says it starts when the thinking changed." Eric pinned the next card lower, deliberate, giving it weight.

"Thinking is an externality," Alexane said. "It doesn't cost anything. Nobody invaded anybody over a telegram." She sorted her cards. "Mine says you need a public act. Policy, money, commitments." She found the card she wanted and held it up so the wind wouldn't take it. "The Truman Doctrine, March 1947. He pledged US support for countries resisting communist pressure. Started with aid to Greece and Turkey. Four hundred million dollars' worth of committing, if you want cost."

"You added the number," Eric said.

"It's on my card, not in the fact." She offered it anyway, and he read it twice, the wind lifting the corner against his thumb.

He wanted the telegram to be the start. It was cleaner, quieter, the war beginning in private understanding before it hardened into public machinery. But he could feel the weakness of it even as he defended it, because a mood was not an event, and a pledge was. If nothing changed in the world when Kennan typed his cable, then what exactly had begun? He unpinned his start card and moved it beside hers, February and March sitting a year apart, and the gap between them was the gap between his two historians, one arguing for the inner turn and the other for the outer one.

"Maybe neither," Maggie said. She had been quiet, warming her hands on the thermos. "Maybe it's like this thing." She tapped the granite soldier's boot. "Nobody can say which day this war started either. They just know it was over when they built him."

"That's not an argument," Eric said, and immediately regretted the flatness of it, because it was an argument, just not one he could pin to a line.

He studied the two cards. The telegram was interpretation; the doctrine was action, and action was what a timeline could hold. But the telegram came first, and first things mattered, and he could not prove they didn't. He pinned them both to the middle of the string, side by side, unranked, and wrote in the margin of his notebook: start contested, evidence favors the public act, certainty not available. It felt like losing and like the first honest thing he had written all week.

Alexane leaned over to read it. "You're conceding."

"I'm withholding judgment."

"That's what people say when they're conceding."

Mr. Holloway came up the path with his dog, saw the timeline strung across the memorial, and stopped. He read the two cards, both pinned mid-string, neither at the beginning, and Eric waited to be corrected or praised, some verdict that would settle the thing. Instead Mr. Holloway took out his phone and photographed the cards side by side. "This is going on the class page," he said. "Thursday's debate topic." He was already walking away, the dog pulling him toward the gate. "Alexane, you're arguing the telegram. Eric, you've got the doctrine. Switched it this morning."

Alexane looked at Eric. Eric looked at his notebook, where his conclusion now argued against his own card, and began unpinning everything.

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: An argument is valid when it is impossible for all its premises to be true and its conclusion false; validity depends only on the argument's form, not on whether the premises are true.
story:
The seminar room smelled of whiteboard marker and radiator dust, and the desks had been pushed into a ragged oval, which Ms. Bear claimed encouraged dialogue but which mostly encouraged Emiliano to lean back until his chair creaked. The topic on the board was "What makes an argument good?" and Carson had come in with a speech half-formed in his head, because he needed this one. His grade in the class was a thin thread, and Ms. Bear had told him that participation in seminar was the knot that would hold or slip.

"Here's one," Emiliano said, tapping his pen against the desk. "All dragons breathe fire. Everything that breathes fire is igneous, basically made of rock that cooled from melting. Smaug is a dragon. Therefore Smaug is igneous. Is that a good argument?"

"That's stupid," Maelie said. "Dragons aren't real. You can't argue about something that doesn't exist."

Carson's hand was up before he had fully decided. "It's not about whether it's real, though." He heard his own voice go careful, the way it did when he was building something he wasn't sure would hold. "Think about it like this. If the premises were true, if all dragons really did breathe fire, and Smaug really was a dragon, could the conclusion be false? Smaug couldn't not be fire-breathing. It's impossible for all the premises to be true and the conclusion false. That's what makes it valid."

"Valid doesn't mean true," Carson added, before anyone could cut in. "The premises are false. Dragons don't exist, so the whole thing is fiction. But the argument is still valid, because validity only depends on the form. It doesn't care whether the premises are true."

Maelie turned her water bottle slowly in her hands, the way she did when she was reorganizing her objections. "So you're saying a good argument can be about nothing."

"I'm saying a valid argument can be about nothing," Carson said, and heard the distinction land somewhere in the room, small and exact. "Good is a different question."

Ms. Bear, who had been sitting at the edge of the oval saying almost nothing, wrote two words on a scrap of paper and slid it across to Carson. Valid. Sound. "For later," she said, and turned to Emiliano. "Give us another example, one where the premises are actually true."

Emiliano sat forward, chair legs clacking down. "Fine. All birds are descended from dinosaurs. Phylogeny puts birds inside the dinosaur family tree. A sparrow is a bird. Therefore sparrows are dinosaurs." He looked around, almost daring someone to object. "That one's real and it's valid."

Carson found himself checking it against the structure Emiliano had used for dragons, the same skeleton under different skin, and the checking felt like something he could do, like a handhold. He thought of his father, who dismissed whole arguments because he didn't like where they came from, and of himself last week, refusing a point in class simply because Maelie had made it first. He had been treating arguments like territories to defend instead of machines to inspect.

"Both your arguments subsume under the same form," Carson said. "Dragons, sparrows, it doesn't matter. You could swap in anything and the validity holds, or it doesn't, based on the shape alone." Then, because the thread he was hanging his grade on felt suddenly worth testing, he added, "But here's what I'm still not sure about. If validity doesn't care about truth, then what's it for? Why do we care that an argument's shape is right when its contents can be lies?"

The room went quiet in the way it did when a question was actually a question. Maelie wrote something in her notebook and turned it so Carson could read it: so that when premises ARE true, the conclusion has to be. He read it twice. That was the conditional heart of it, the promise folded inside the form: if the inputs check out, the output is guaranteed, and if they don't, nothing is owed. He could feel the shape of a considered position assembling itself, Emiliano's silliness and Maelie's skepticism and his own need to be right, all of it fit together except the last piece, which stayed loose.

He said, "Okay. So a valid argument with true premises is the thing we actually want, and validity alone is just, I don't know, the chassis. And I can't tell, yet, whether knowing that makes arguments better or just makes me more careful about them. Maybe both. Maybe that's the cost."

Ms. Bear underlined something twice in her book of names and grades, and Carson watched her pen, unable to tell whether the thread had held or slipped. Maelie capped her pen and said, "Sparrows are dinosaurs, though. That part's just true."

"Prove it," Emiliano said, and grinned, and turned a fresh page in his notebook.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Under US federal child labor rules, workers under 18 may not operate power-driven meat slicers, even in a grocery store deli or restaurant.
story:
The application had taken Savannah forty minutes in the corner of the grocery store by the coupon rack, and the manager, a broad man with reading glasses pushed up on his forehead, had hired her before she'd finished her water. Saturday orientation, he said. Deli counter, minimum wage, show up in black shoes. She walked out through the automatic doors into the smell of hot asphalt and quartered watermelon, and texted her mother from the parking lot, grinning at nothing.

Orientation turned out to be a folding table behind the bakery, a stack of laminated sheets, and Mr. Oyelaran, who had worked the deli for nineteen years and had opinions about everything, most of them gentle. He walked the new hires through the slicer, the fryer, the case temperatures, the scale. When he reached the slicer he rested a hand on its steel carriage the way you'd rest a hand on a horse. "This is the dangerous one," he said. "Respect it and it's honest work." Savannah wrote respect it in her notebook and underlined it twice, mostly to look like the kind of person who underlined things.

The third Saturday, at ten in the morning, the deli got slammed. A youth soccer team had commandeered half the parking lot for a car wash, and their parents, apparently all hungry at once, filled the counter three deep with tickets for turkey and provolone and Land O Lakes, half a pound, shaved. Mr. Oyelaran was called away to receive a delivery, and Brittany, the other new hire, had called in sick with what her voicemail described as "a situation." That left Savannah and Lexus, who was friendly and quick and had been at the store two months, and who was, Savannah happened to know from the break room, seventeen. Her birthday was pinned to the corkboard because the whole staff signed cards.

Lexus pulled the first ticket, keyed in the order, and reached for the slicer's start switch without hesitation. The case was full of waiting faces, the fryer ticking behind them, the number display climbing toward forty minutes of wait time, and somewhere in the noise Savannah felt a cold edge of foreboding, the same feeling she'd had at fifteen when a friend's older brother handed her the keys to a truck.

She'd said no that night, and ridden home in the dark with her bike lamp dying, embarrassed the whole way. Her father, when she told him, had only nodded and said the law was on her side even when it felt like an insult, and she'd thought about that for years afterward, how a rule could be both protective and humiliating at once.

"Wait," Savannah said now, and put her hand flat on the slicer's guard. Lexus looked at her, ticket still in her teeth. "You're seventeen, right?" Lexus nodded, wary. "I think it's illegal. Under federal child labor rules, workers under eighteen can't operate power-driven meat slicers, not even in a grocery store deli or a restaurant. That's the whole rule, I read it when I got hired because it scared me." Lexus took the ticket out of her teeth. "Then who does the slicing?"

"I do," Savannah said, and discovered as she said it that she was already scared in the good way, the way that makes your hands careful. She set the thickness dial, locked the carriage, fed the first wedge of turkey through while Lexus ran the scale, bagged, called numbers, and cracked jokes about soccer parents in a whisper that made the line laugh despite itself. Savannah kept her knuckles clear of the blade and her eyes on the cut, and thought, in the gaps between orders, that the law was a blunt instrument and also, this morning, exactly the right one.

When Mr. Oyelaran came back the line was gone and Lexus was wiping down the case. He looked at the clean slicer, then at Savannah, then at the corkboard with the birthdays, and something shifted behind his glasses. "Who cut the eight orders?" "I did," Savannah said. "Lexus did everything else." He was quiet for a moment, and she couldn't tell whether he was grateful or annoyed at having been caught in a gap he should have seen himself. "Good," he said finally. "Keep it that way." He picked up the stack of tickets and squared it against the counter.

At break, outside on the milk crates by the loading dock, Lexus split a package of gas station cookies with her and said, "You didn't have to make it a thing. You could've just said you wanted the slicer." Savannah turned that over, because she hadn't wanted it, and yet she had wanted something, the feeling of being the one who could. "Next summer it's yours," she said. "The whole slicer." Lexus laughed, and the sun came off the ice machine in bright little shards across the asphalt, and inside, over the speaker, someone paged the deli again.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: In the tabling method, melted chocolate is spread and worked on a cool marble slab to bring its temperature down and start stable crystals forming.
story:
The problem presented itself on the second Tuesday of the unit, when Carson unmolded his chocolate shells and they came out dull as old pavement, bending instead of snapping. Around him, Logan's shells gave a clean click when he tapped them together, and Jolie held hers up to the window light with a smugness she didn't bother hiding. Ms. Anderson walked the aisles with her hands clasped behind her back, pausing at Carson's station only long enough to say, "Temper," and move on, as if the single word were a diagnosis.

The word followed him home. He understood that untempered chocolate was a failure of patience rather than skill, or maybe the other way around, and that afternoon he sat at his laptop collating videos and forum posts, arranging them side by side the way he would arrange evidence for a debate. There were two main methods, it turned out. Seed method, where you chopped in cold chocolate to cool the melt. And another, older one, which the videos demonstrated on slabs of pale stone.

"Tabling," his friend Logan said that Thursday, when Carson described it at lunch. "My uncle does it. He spreads the melted chocolate on a cold marble slab and works it around with scrapers until it comes down to temperature." Logan tore the crust off his sandwich as he talked. "He says it's the real way, not this seeding shortcut."

"Shortcut isn't a dysphemism for easier," Jolie said, without looking up from her phone. "It's just accurate." She and Logan had this argument in some form most days, and Carson had learned to hold his part of the table like a border checkpoint, letting the traffic pass both ways. Privately he sided with Jolie on most things, because she was usually right, and privately he wanted what Logan's uncle had, which was the old way, the flourished way, chocolate moved in ribbons across cool stone.

"Come Saturday," Logan said. "My uncle's got the shop and there's a slab in the back. He won't mind."

What Logan actually had was an empty house, an uncle two towns over, and a granite countertop in the kitchen that stayed cold no matter how long the heating ran. "It's stone," Logan said, thumping it. "Same principle." Carson laid his hand on the surface. It was cool, not cold, and he had no marble and no thermometer and only one bar of decent chocolate, but he'd melted it in a bowl over a pot of water and carried it across town wrapped in a towel like something stolen.

"Spread it," Logan said, and Carson poured. The chocolate ran out in a dark rope and Carson worked it with a spatula, pushing it flat across the granite, gathering it back, spreading again, the way the videos had shown. The stone pulled the heat out of it visibly, the sheen dulling and thickening as he moved. "Tabling," Logan announced, as though naming a magic trick. "On a cool stone. That's how you bring the temperature down and get the crystals forming. That's the whole thing."

Carson felt peevish about the word crystals, since Logan had spent ten minutes at lunch calling them "crystals" in air quotes, but he said nothing, because something was happening under the spatula. The chocolate was thickening toward fudge, and in the videos it always loosened again when the worker folded it back into the warm bowl. He scraped his pile up and stirred it in, and it did loosen, and he spread it again on the stone and worked it back, twice more, until the chocolate held a gloss it hadn't had before and set on his fingertip in less than a minute, dry and slightly tacky-free, if that was a word, which it wasn't.

They poured it onto parchment in careless pools and bars, and while it set Jolie texted Carson a photo of her seeded batch from home, glossy as a beetle's back, with the caption "still faster." He turned the phone toward Logan, who looked at it for a long moment and then got out plates.

Logan's stone countertop was not marble, and the kitchen was warmer than any chocolatier would allow, and half their bars bloomed with pale streaks by morning, which Logan's uncle, reached by phone, attributed in a single sentence to "working it warm." But two bars out of six had snapped clean, a sound like a knuckle cracking, and their broken faces shone. Carson turned one of them over in the light and understood that he couldn't actually choose between the methods, because the seeding had worked at school for Jolie while he'd failed, and the tabling had worked at Logan's while half of it failed, and the difference was probably not the method at all but the hand and the room, neither of which he controlled.

On Monday he told Ms. Anderson he wanted to try both again, properly, with a thermometer, and she said, "Then you'll need two batches," and wrote him a pass for the lab on Wednesday. He sat down between Logan and Jolie, who had already resumed their argument about shortcuts, and began breaking his failed shells into a bowl for remelting.

"Snap test," Jolie said, sliding one of her shells across the counter to him.

Carson broke it, listened, and started his double boiler.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In Arthur Aron's 1997 study, pairs of strangers took turns asking each other 36 questions that grew gradually more personal, and they ended up feeling closer than pairs making small talk.
story:
I have never been nervous in my life, which is why my hands were perfectly steady while I waited at the counter of the shop on Millward Street, and why I had rehearsed nothing, and why I checked my phone four times in six minutes. He was late, but only a little, and when he came through the door shaking rain off his jacket I felt nothing at all except the ordinary recognition of a boy from my chemistry class, the one whose name I had definitely known for months and not looked up on three separate platforms last night.

"You got mint?" he said, reading the board over my head. "Good. Everyone who likes mint chip is trustworthy."

"That's not true," I said. "I like mint chip."

He laughed and paid before I could, which I let him do because arguing about money on a first date seemed like a worse opening than accepting it. We took the corner booth by the window. For a while it went the way these things go: the toppings bar, the quiz on Friday, the fact that Mr. Zhao had moved the exam again, and did he think Zhao enjoyed watching us suffer, and yes, obviously, the man had an ascetic streak, he'd once confiscated a birthday cake in tenth grade on the grounds that frosting was a distraction. I was doing well. I was carrying the conversation the way you carry a full tray, level and unhurried, and I knew exactly what I was doing.

Then the tray wobbled. We ran out of quiz, out of toppings, out of Mr. Zhao. He scraped his spoon around the bottom of his cup and I watched the window fog and unfog with somebody's breath on the other side of it, and neither of us said anything, and I understood that everything I had prepared, which was nothing, had been used up.

"Okay," I said, because I am decisive. "We could just do small talk until one of us pretends we have homework."

"Or," he said.

"Or there's this thing. A psychologist, Arthur Aron, in 1997, he did a study where pairs of strangers took turns asking each other thirty-six questions, and the questions got gradually more personal as they went. The pairs who did that ended up feeling closer than the pairs who just made small talk."

He looked at me with his spoon stopped halfway to his mouth. "Where did you read that?"

"My friend Pearl printed it out and taped it inside my locker this morning, which I am telling you because she'll walk past that window eventually and I'd rather you hear it from me." This was almost true. Pearl had taped it there in March, before the last dance, and I had left it up all this time because I liked the look of it, and I had memorized the questions in June, and I had selected this boy partly, though not entirely, from a shortlist. "Do you want to try it? We can stop anytime."

"Question one," he said immediately, which I took as a good sign and did not examine.

The first questions were easy, almost silly. Given the choice of anyone in the world, whom would you want as a dinner guest. We both wasted our answers on dead physicists. What would constitute a perfect day for you, and his was so specific, involving a lake and a particular bakery and his grandmother's dog, that I felt something shift in my chest like a drawer sliding open. I gave a vaguer answer and covered by calling my perfect day ascetic compared to his, all silence and library, and he said he didn't believe me, and I said he was right not to, and then had to sit with what I'd admitted.

Around question twenty the mint chip was gone and the shop had emptied except for a woman behind the counter refilling the sprinkles. He told me about the thing with his brother, the one he never told anyone, the peccadillo that wasn't really small at all but had gotten labeled small at home until the label stuck. I told him about my mother's kitchen and what it sounded like at two in the morning, which I had told Pearl and no one else. He did not try to fix it. He just asked what the fridge sounded like, exactly, and I described the hum, and he nodded like that was a reasonable thing to want to know.

Somewhere past question thirty I noticed I had stopped performing. This was the part Pearl's printout hadn't warned me about, or maybe it had and I hadn't read the margins: closeness comes in like a tide and takes things out with it when it goes. He knew things now. He could carry them anywhere, to chemistry on Monday, to the group chat, into whatever version of me he decided to invent later. I had spent years being perfectly steady, and I had just handed a near-stranger the evidence.

"Last one," he said. "Of the people in your family, whose death would you find most disturbing, and why."

"Whichever one I could have prevented," I said. He held my eyes for a second too long, and I let him.

Outside, the rain had stopped. The woman at the counter turned the sign, and Pearl appeared at the window, waved, and kept walking. He pulled the paper from my locker out of my bag, looked at the creases, and folded it back along the same lines.

"Same time next week," he said. "Question thirty-seven."

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: In Peter Wason's 1966 selection task, people must pick which cards to turn over to test an if-then rule; in his study, fewer than 10 percent chose the correct cards in the abstract version.
story:
Jordyn arrived early to fourth period because Ms. Georgiou had promised a puzzle, and Jordyn liked puzzles the way some people liked thunderstorms, from a safe distance with the lights on. The desks had been pushed into a crooked horseshoe. On the board, four oversized cards stood in a row: A, D, 4, 7. Beside them, in Ms. Georgiou's tidy hand, was written: If a card has a vowel on one side, then it has an even number on the other side. Your job: decide which cards you must turn over to test whether the rule holds.

"Only the ones you need," Ms. Georgiou said, tapping the marker against her palm. "This is called the selection task. It comes from Peter Wason, 1966." She handed out slips of paper. "Write your letters and numbers, fold them, pass them forward. No conferring."

Jordyn wrote A and 4 almost without thinking. The A was obvious; turn it over, look for the even number. The 4 felt like due diligence. She folded her slip and watched Samuel hunch over his, chewing his pen, and Brent raise his hand before the slips had even reached the desk.

"If I turn the A and it has a 4 under it, doesn't that prove it?"

"It tells you something," Ms. Georgiou said, and slid the slips into a coffee mug. "Let's see what we all said." She unfolded them one at a time, reading aloud. A and 4, A and 4, A and 4, A alone, A and 4 and 7. Brent had written A and 4 and every other card, which he defended loudly, saying that checking everything couldn't hurt. Samuel, when his slip came up, had written A and 4 like Jordyn, and he turned around in his seat and grinned at her as if they'd won something together.

Ms. Georgiou counted. "Out of twenty-six slips, two are correct." She let the silence sit. "In Wason's original study, in the abstract version like this one, fewer than ten percent of people chose the correct cards." She set the mug down. "I'm not going to tell you which two cards. That's your homework: figure out what you'd need to see to know the rule is false, not just to see it confirmed again."

The bell rang on the word false, and it followed Jordyn down the hallway like a stray. At lunch she sat with Samuel and Brent in the cafeteria, where Brent was staging his usual protest against the lasagna, pushing it around the tray and declaring that he refused to be an epicure in a place with epicurean ambitions and cardboard supplies. Samuel ignored him. He had spread a napkin on the table and copied the four cards onto it in blue ink. "So we were wrong," he said. "Both of us. Same wrong."

"Everyone's wrong the same way," Jordyn said, but she was barely listening to herself. She pulled the napkin toward her and drew a line down the middle. One side she labeled could prove it, the other, could break it. The A went on the proving side. Then the 4. Then she stopped, pen hovering. She turned the 4 over in her mind and saw that whatever was on the back, a vowel or a consonant, the rule survived. The 4 couldn't break anything. It was a mirror she'd been polishing for no reason.

"Try the 7," she said slowly. Samuel frowned. "If there's a vowel under the 7, the rule's dead. A vowel with an odd number. That's the thing we're not allowed to find." Brent leaned across his abandoned lasagna, interested despite himself, and flipped an imaginary 7 with his finger. "D under there, rule's fine. A under there, rule's broken. So the 7 is a real test." Jordyn felt the small cold thrill of it. "So it's A and 7. We check the case that could disprove it, not the case that flatters it."

That night she lay on her bed with her phone above her face and typed a message to Samuel, then deleted it, then typed again. "I keep thinking about how fast I wrote A and 4. Like my hand already knew the answer before I did. Except it didn't know, it just wanted to be right. I want to know if I do that other places. Not cards. Other places." She stared at the words. It sounded like something a person with a library and a sweater vest would say. She added, "Also Brent says the diner on Mercer has real milkshakes, Friday, if you're in," and pressed send before she could revise herself into silence.

Samuel replied with a thumbs up and then, a minute later: "A and 7. Ms. G. marked my napkin homework and gave me a check mark with a question mark next to it, which I think means I explained it badly but got it right." Then: "Friday yes." Jordyn set the phone on her chest. Somewhere below the window a car door slammed, and the smell of someone's charcoal dinner drifted up through the screen, smoky and ordinary. She thought about the 4, glossy and obedient, showing its harmless face, and about all the 7s she had never turned over, in arguments with her mother, in the college essay she'd written to say what she thought they wanted to hear. On Friday, over milkshakes, she would start with Brent's theory that the cafeteria was a conspiracy and see if she could find the card that could prove him wrong. She picked up the phone and typed, "Bring the napkin."

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: Near the end of the development, a retransition often dwells on the home key's dominant chord, building an expectation that the tonic and the first theme are about to return.
story:
The music room smelled of radiator dust and old sheet music, and Amy had spread the Mozart score across two desks pushed together so the pages would lie flat. She had three coloured pencils: blue for the exposition, green for the development, orange for the recapitulation, and so far she had only the blue down, a confident line after the repeat sign where the second theme finally settled somewhere new.

"What happens if you get it wrong?" Amber asked from the piano bench, where she was picking out a pop song by ear, one note at a time.

"Mr. He says the analysis is worth less than the listening," Amy said. "But that's the kind of thing a teacher says when he's already decided the analysis matters most."

Amber gave her a sardonic look. "You could just enjoy it."

"I do enjoy it. I want to know why." Amy had been proselytizing about this for weeks, cornering anyone who would stand still: that theory wasn't the opposite of feeling, it was a way of finding out where the feeling came from. Amber had heard the sermon enough times to hum it back at her.

Quinten came in with his viola case and sat down without asking, which was how he joined conversations. He leaned over her score. "So where's the development end?"

"That's the problem. It doesn't announce itself. It just... stops being one thing and starts being another." She played the recording on her phone, the movement's opening, and watched Amber abandon her pop song to listen despite herself.

The three of them went to the concert that Friday because Mr. He had offered extra credit and because Amy had decided, privately, that extra credit was only the excuse. The hall was small, the piano close enough that they could see the pianist's hands. During the first movement of a different Mozart sonata, Amy sat with the score folded shut in her lap, having promised herself she would listen the way Amber listened, without a map. Near the end of the middle section the harmony narrowed to a single insistently repeated chord, and she found herself leaning forward in her seat, certain the opening tune was about to come back. Beside her, Quinten leaned forward too, at exactly the same moment, and when the first theme did return, brighter than before, he turned to her with his eyebrows up as if to say, how did we know?

Afterwards, on the bus, she worked it out aloud, half to Quinten and half to herself. "It wasn't guessing. The music was doing something, right at the end of the middle part. It stayed on that chord like it was waiting."

"Dominant," Quinten said. "Mr. He called that bit the retransition, once, and then he shut up about it."

"Of course he did." Amy stared out the window at the lit fronts of houses sliding past. She had been treating the analysis like a filing system, blue and green and orange, but the thing that had pulled her forward in her seat was not a label. It was the chord dwelling on the home key's dominant, building the expectation that the tonic and the first theme were coming, and they had both felt it without any pencil at all. The two ways of knowing hadn't been competing. Or maybe they had been, and she couldn't yet say which one had known first.

Monday she found Mr. He tuning the piano in the music room, the room humming with the A. She laid her score on the stand with the blue line, the green line she had now drawn, and a question mark where the orange should begin, a few bars before the theme actually returns.

"That's where I leaned forward," she said. "Friday, at the concert. Is that where the mark goes, or where my mark goes?"

Mr. He played the passage, the harmony circling, refusing to move, and let his hand rest on the key. "You're asking whether the analysis is where the chord is or where the listener is."

"I'm asking if they're the same thing."

He didn't answer that, and she found she didn't want him to. She took the orange pencil, held it over the bar, and listened to him play the passage again, letting herself fall into the reverie of it even with her eyes open, watching her own hand hover.

She drew the line where the chord began to dwell, then drew a second small mark where the theme came back, and left the gap between them blank. Amber, arriving late with her earbuds still in, looked over her shoulder and said, "You made it messier."

"I made it true," Amy said, and played the opening theme on the piano with one hand, badly, and played it again.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: Behavioral interview questions, such as 'Tell me about a time when...', are built on the idea that past behavior is a good predictor of future behavior.
story:
The bus pulled out of the lot at 3:12, and Mathis had the printed page folded into quarters in his jacket pocket, though he knew what it said without looking. Interview, Saturday, 10:00 a.m., Halstead's Pharmacy. Bring references. He had no references. He had a mother who had written his only one on a sticky note and signed it with her maiden name, which he had not decided yet whether to use.

"You're staring at the emergency exit like it's going to open for you," Tori said, sliding into the seat beside him without asking, the way she did every day. She took the page from his pocket before he could object and smoothed it on her knee. "Part-time clerk. Okay. So they'll ask you things and you'll answer them. You've done harder things."

"Name one."

She tilted her head, conceding the point, and pulled out her phone. "Then we practice. That's all an interview is, practice that counts. Sit up. Look at me like I'm a man named Halstead with a mustache."

He sat up. He looked at her, and the bus swayed through the long suburban turns while she read questions off some hiring website, and his answers kept dying halfway out of his mouth. Asked to describe a strength, he mumbled something about being responsible. Asked why he wanted the job, he said money, which was true and, apparently, wrong.

"Here's the part you're messing up," Tori said, turning the phone toward him. "These are behavioral questions. They all start the same way, tell me about a time when. They're built on the idea that past behavior is a good predictor of future behavior. So they don't care what you'd do. They want what you did."
