Mathis read the screen twice. It was the kind of sentence that sounded obvious until you had to act on it, and now, acting on it, he found he had nothing. He had never worked. There had been a summer of mowing the neighbor's lawn, paid in cash and lemonade, and one occasion in tenth grade when he spoke at Mr. Nair's retirement assembly, an unplanned eulogy for a living man, three minutes about a chemistry teacher whose desk was famously ascetic, nothing on it ever but a grade book and a single dried-out pen. The school had afterward handed him a small honorarium for addressing the incoming freshmen about study habits, twenty dollars in a card, and he had felt important for exactly one afternoon.

"I have school stuff," he said. "Does school stuff count?"

"That's what you have, so it has to."

"Then it counts." He heard his own voice land with more force than he'd intended, and Tori raised an eyebrow, approving.

They ran it again. Tell me about a time you handled a conflict: the group project where Kaya had refused to rewrite her section and he had sat with her after class and cut it apart line by line until she chose her own cuts, which he described now with his chin up and his eyes on Tori's and his hands still on his knees. Tell me about a time you failed: the exam he'd walked into having read the wrong chapters, the recovery plan he'd made, the follow-up he'd actually done. Each answer was true. Each one, he noticed, also made him sound more deliberate than he'd been at the time, and when he said so, Tori shrugged.

"That's not lying, that's selection. Everybody's a list of times and you're picking which ones to show."

He wasn't sure that was right, either, but the bus was slowing for his stop and there was no time to argue it. He took the page back, folded it along its old creases, and stood in the aisle holding the rail. He felt prepared, and the feeling was thin in a way he couldn't name, like knowing the route but not the traffic.

"Saturday," Tori said from the window as he stepped down. "Mustache. Chin up. Past behavior."

"Predicts future behavior," he said, and the doors closed on her laugh.

He stood on the curb until the bus turned the corner. In his pocket the folded page was soft at the edges already, and he thought again about the honorarium card, which he had kept, and about whether the man from that one afternoon was someone he could promise to keep being. The porch light was on. He took the porch steps two at a time and reached, before he went in, for his phone to text Kaya: do you remember that project.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: Under US federal law, workers aged 16 and 17 have no limit on working hours but may not be employed in jobs the Department of Labor has declared hazardous.
story:
Arianna sat on the dock with her knees pulled up, watching Faisal fold his interview notes into smaller and smaller squares. The counselors had set up mock interviews all week, part of the camp's "real world readiness" unit, and Arianna had volunteered to go last, hoping the unit might end before her turn arrived. It had not.

"I looked at the floor the whole time," Faisal said. "Ms. Santos-Reyes said I mumbled my availability." He flicked the folded square into the lake, then thought better of it and waded in to retrieve it, because littering was the kind of thing that got you kitchen duty here, and kitchen duty was where Arianna was headed next.

She went early to peel potatoes, and it was there, over the slicer, that she overheard the two kitchen staff arguing. The older one, a college student home for the summer, wanted his Thursday shift covered. The younger one, seventeen and quiet, said he would take it, and the older one said great, you can run the slicer, I'll show you once and then it's yours. The quiet one looked at the machine the way Arianna looked at her interview notes, and said nothing.

Arianna had acclimated to the kitchen's noise over the past two weeks, to the clatter and the radio and the cook's habit of narrating everything he did, but something about the offer snagged her. She had read a flyer in the camp office, the one about youth employment laws that somebody had tacked up beside the schedule board, mostly out of boredom on a rainy afternoon. She remembered almost none of it, except a shape of an idea, like remembering that a room had a blue chair without remembering the room.

She found Ms. Santos-Reyes by the flagpole before dinner and asked, without quite knowing how to start, whether there were rules about what teenagers could do at jobs. Ms. Santos-Reyes smiled in a way that suggested this was the first interesting question anyone had asked her all week and said the office had the actual materials, and that Arianna was welcome to look, and that she should tell her what she found. That was all. No lecture. Arianna liked her for it.

In the office, under the hum of the old refrigerator, Arianna read the page twice. Workers aged sixteen and seventeen had no limit on working hours. She read that sentence again because it contradicted what she had assumed, some vague curfew of her imagination. But the same page said they could not be employed in jobs the Department of Labor had declared hazardous, and there was a list, and power-driven meat slicers were on it. She sat with the folder open for a long moment, caught between two instincts. One said tell someone, quickly. The other said mind your own business, you've known these people for two weeks, you're sixteen, the older staff member will think you're showing off or lecturing him, and he had a temper that could turn vitriolic over small things like burnt toast.

At breakfast she did neither. She carried her tray past the quiet seventeen-year-old, whose name she had never learned, and put it down across from him, and said, "Did you take that Thursday shift?" He said maybe. She said, "I read something in the office about our age group. Sixteen and seventeen, no limit on hours, but some jobs are off limits. Slicers are on the list." She kept her eyes on his, the way she had not managed to do in her own mock interview, and it was easier here, somehow, because she was not asking for anything.

He looked at his eggs. "He'll be mad."

"Maybe," Arianna said. "You could tell him it's the law, not you."

By the time the morning dishes were done, word had traveled the way it does in a camp this size, a milieu small enough that three people knowing a thing meant everyone did. The college student cornered Arianna by the dish rack. She braced for it. Instead he said the cook had found the same page taped inside a cabinet, of all places, and that Thursday was now his problem again, and that he guessed he owed her a soda. He did not say thank you exactly. He set a can of orange soda on the counter beside her, still cold, and walked back to the sinks.

That afternoon was her make-up interview, the last slot of the unit. Ms. Santos-Reyes asked her the standard questions, and Arianna answered most of them badly, still, her hands still doing too much, her "teamwork" example still thin. But when asked to describe a time she had solved a problem, she found she could look straight across the table and say the whole thing plainly, the flyer, the folder, the breakfast conversation, the parts that worked and the part that had not, the older boy's pride she might have bruised. At the end Ms. Santos-Reyes said, "That one I believed," and started stacking the papers, and outside the window Faisal was sitting on the dock again, holding what looked like a fresh set of notes, waving her out.

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: Historian Frances Wood argued that Marco Polo may never have reached China, pointing out that his book never mentions tea, foot-binding or the Great Wall.
story:
The folding tables had been pushed together into one long surface, and Addison's grandmother's lasagna sat at the center of it like a hostage. Around it, aunts argued about whose turn it was to host Thanksgiving, and Addison kept her backpack against her chair, because inside it was a library book she had checked out for her history report, and inside that book was a problem she could not stop chewing on.

"Marco Polo," her grandfather was saying, spooning himself a second portion. "Now there was a man. Seventeen years in China. Wrote the whole thing down."

Addison set down her fork. "Actually, there's a historian who thinks he maybe never got there at all."

The table went quiet in the way it did when someone said something at the wrong volume. Her uncle laughed, but her grandfather's eyebrows came down like a gate.

"Never got there? The man wrote a book about it."

"That's the thing," Addison said. "Frances Wood, she's a historian, she argued that Marco Polo may never have reached China. Because his book never mentions tea, or foot-binding, or the Great Wall. Things you'd think you couldn miss if you'd actually been there."

"Absurd," her grandfather said. "He didn't miss them. You're missing them."

Under the table, she texted Iyad, who was doing his report on the same unit: did you know about the Marco Polo thing?? The response came before she finished her potatoes: YES. Keira's already picked a side. Keira always picks a side.

That was true, and it was what had been bothering Addison all week, though she hadn't had the words for it until now, watching the gravy boat travel down the table. Keira had announced in the library that Polo was obviously a liar, the way she announced everything, and Iyad had pushed back just as hard, and the two of them had gone at it until Mr. Holloway, who supervised the study hall, had come over to see what the argument was. He hadn't settled it. He'd only asked what sources they were using, which at the time had felt like a dodge and now, under the fluorescent lights of her grandmother's dining room, felt like the most honest thing anyone had said.

The flashback arrived without warning, the way hers always did. Fourth grade, the family reunion at the lake, and she had sworn to her cousins that she had seen a turtle the size of a car door off the dock. She had seen something. Her cousin had seen a log. For years they'd fought about it at every gathering, and it wasn't until last summer that her mother had said, mildly, that maybe both of them were telling the truth about what they'd seen and both of them were wrong about what it was. Addison, thirteen at the time and freshly furious, had called this a cop-out. Now she wasn't so sure it wasn't the most sophisticated position available.

"So which is it," her grandfather said, pulling her back. "Did he go or not? You're the student. Tell us."

"I don't know," she said.

"That's not an answer."

"It kind of is, though." She turned the library book over in her hands, the cover soft from use. "Wood isn't saying he definitely didn't go. She's saying the evidence is weird. He wrote this whole thing, all these grandiose stories about the Khan's court, and he never once mentions tea. Everyone there drinks tea. All day. It's like writing about my grandma's house and never mentioning the lasagna."

Her grandmother pointed her wooden spoon. "Nobody doesn't mention the lasagna."

"Exactly," Addison said. "But here's the other part. Maybe he just forgot things. Maybe he didn't think tea was interesting. Maybe he heard it all secondhand from Persian merchants and wrote it down like he'd been there. Historians fight about this because the book is all we've got. It's one source. One guy. And everybody who reads it asks different questions, so they notice different things. Iyad says the questions historians ask change over time, like what people even care about looking for."

Her uncle smirked. "So the past is whatever you want it to be."

"No," Addison said, and was a little surprised by how firm her voice came out. "The past is what it was. It's the knowing that's crooked."

At the end of the table, her ten-year-old cousin, who had been quietly building with the little plastic bricks their grandmother kept in a basket for exactly this purpose, held up a finished spaceship. "Look. It comes apart into four pieces and goes back together." He demonstrated, pulling it into sections and reassembling it. "You can make different ships with the same parts."

The table admired it, and Addison sat very still, because that was somehow the thing itself, the same parts, different ships, different questions, same China, and she had a paragraph in her head already. Later, in the kitchen, drying dishes while her grandfather washed them in silence, she pulled out her phone and took a photo of the book's cover.

"What's that for?" he asked.

"Sending to Iyad. We're meeting in the library Monday. Keira too."

"Hmph," he said, and handed her the last plate, and it was still warm.

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: The US National Labor Relations Act, signed on July 5, 1935, gave most private-sector workers the right to form unions and bargain collectively.
story:
The kitchen smelled of bleach and fried onions, and Sierra had learned to tell time by the dishes: the lunch rush plates were still greasy with aioli, the dinner ones not yet stacked. She was sixteen, and she'd been hired at Marlowe's for minimum wage with a promise, made casually by the manager in a doorway, that her pay would be "revisited" after a month. Two months had passed. Tonight her mother had texted her twice about the electric bill, and Sierra had wiped her hands on her apron to read the messages, standing between the dish machine and the mop sink where nobody could see her face.

"The schedule's out," Maia said, slamming through the swinging door with a tub of ketchup bottles. Maia was nineteen, a server, saving for a pharmacy tech certificate, and she wanted the Friday closing shift because Friday tips were the only thing standing between her and another semester of waiting tables forever. "Guess who got Thursdays and Sunday lunch. Both of them. Me. Again." She set the tub down hard enough that a bottle tipped over and rolled toward the drain.

"That's the good shift, isn't it?" Sierra asked. "Sunday lunch?"

"Sunday lunch is church crowds who tip like the collection plate already emptied them. Fridays are where the money is, and Renata gets them every single week because she's been here longest and the manager likes her." Maia righted the bottle. "It's not even about seniority, really. There's no rule. There's nothing written down anywhere. It's just whatever he decides that week."

Sierra scraped a plate into the garbage. Her own hours had been cut from thirty a week to nineteen, without warning, the schedule taped up on a Thursday like weather nobody had asked for. She'd asked the manager about the raise and he'd said business was slow, that she should be grateful for clemency, that other places would have let her go entirely. The word had struck her strangely even then; she hadn't committed a crime, only asked for what she'd been promised.

In the break room, folding her apron at midnight, Sierra found Shyanne from the prep line already sitting at the table with her phone out and her boots off. Shyanne was twenty-two and enrolled part-time at the community college, and she talked about her coursework the way other people talked about vacations. "You two look like a labor dispute," she said.

"Can we even do anything?" Maia said. "Like, are we even allowed to complain together? He fired that cook last spring for arguing."

"We're allowed," Shyanne said. "The National Labor Relations Act, signed July 5, 1935, gave most private-sector workers the right to form unions and bargain collectively. I just wrote a paper on it." She turned her phone around so they could see the screen. "I looked it up because of this place, actually. It applies here. We can talk about it, we can organize, we can even vote in a union. It's the law."

Sierra leaned over the tiny screen, scrolling through the statute with her thumb. She had assumed, without ever examining the assumption, that a job was a kind of private arrangement, small and parochial, between her and one manager, and that everything else, hours, tips, the raise, was an act of his personal generosity or its withdrawal. It was almost embarrassing how the idea enraptured her, that there was a whole architecture underneath, older than her grandmother, built for exactly this. At the same time she didn't want to be naive. A law on paper was one thing; a manager who controlled the schedule was another, and she needed nineteen hours, not zero.

"Here," Shyanne said, and slid a folded paper across the table. "Read this tonight. I drafted something." It was a letter, handwritten, addressed to the manager, and Sierra read it while Maia read over her shoulder. It laid out what they wanted, in plain sentences: a written schedule posted two weeks in advance, a tip pool for Friday closers instead of one person's arrangement, a wage review with dates. At the bottom it said, "We are aware of our rights under federal labor law and are submitting this together." Below that, three blank lines for signatures, and under those, a fourth and a fifth, because Shyanne was thinking of Renata and the prep cooks too, everyone whose wants ran alongside theirs even when they didn't say so.

Maia picked up the pen first. She pressed it against the paper and looked up at Sierra, and her hand hovered there, and outside the break room door the dish machine hissed through its final cycle of the night. Sierra wiped her palms on her jeans and reached for the pen.

"If we both sign, he'll know it was all three of us," she said.

"He already knows we talk," Maia said. "This just makes it official." She signed, quick and slanted, and slid the paper across the table until it sat under the light, waiting.

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: Congress can override a US president's veto with a two-thirds vote in both the House and the Senate.
story:
The bill began as a page of Xavier's handwriting on the library table, next to a half-eaten apple and a printout about hepatitis A cases at the riverfront shelters. He had underlined the word epidemiology twice, because the county health report used it in every paragraph and he wanted to be sure he was using it correctly: the study of how disease spread through that population of people, who used the one working fountain at the skate park because the shelters' water had been shut off in June.

"Read the title again," Athena said, pulling the page toward her. Willy sat on the far side of the table with his laptop open, headphones around his neck, leaking a thin drumbeat into the room.

"An Act to Restore Public Water Access at Recreational Facilities in the County," Xavier said. "Mr. Nkosi said a bill has to be drafted in the language it would actually appear in, not just described. Every clause."

Mr. Nkosi was the reference librarian, and he had agreed to run the simulation for their civics class again this year. He kept a rubber stamp at the desk that said ASSENT, and a wooden gavel he had brought from home, and he did not lecture. On the first day he had handed each of them a card: Xavier and Athena drawn for the Senate, Willy for the House, two dozen other classmates distributed between the chambers by cards drawn from a coffee tin.

The committee hearing took place at the long table by the microfilm cabinets, because it was the only table big enough. Athena chaired it. A girl from the opposing party moved to strike the section requiring quarterly inspections, calling it burdensome, and Willy, who was not even in that committee but had wandered over, said the section was germane or it wasn't, and the inspection requirement clearly related to water safety, so the motion to strike it as off-topic failed anyway. The committee reported the bill out with amendments. Athena signed the report. Xavier watched her do it, the pen pressing through onto the table's wood grain.

Debate on the floor was held the following Tuesday, after school, in the reading room with its tall windows and the smell of old carpet and lemon floor polish. Mr. Nkosi had ruled that the Senate would sit at the round tables near the window and the House across the aisle by the biography shelves, and that any member could speak for two minutes. A boy argued the county could not afford the plumbing. Xavier argued back with the health report, holding it up, reading the case counts aloud, his voice going flat in the way it did when he was nervous. The vote in the Senate was fourteen to six. Willy texted him from the House side: 19 to 11 over here. Both chambers had passed it. Athena stamped the pages in order.

Then Mr. Nkosi cleared his throat and took out a red pen. He was the president in the simulation too, apparently, and he had read the bill overnight. He wrote two words on the back of the title page and slid it across the desk: VETO returned. He rang the gavel once and walked back to the reference desk, where a woman was asking him how to transliterate her grandmother's maiden name from Cyrillic script into English for a passport application, and he helped her letter by letter.

The three of them sat in the study carrels with the lights overhead humming. Willy said the whole thing was dead, then, and started packing his bag. Athena said wait. She had the card with the chamber counts written on it, and she turned it over and looked at it for a long moment.

"It can go back," she said. "Congress can override a president's veto with a two-thirds vote in both the House and the Senate. I read it in the textbook. It just has to be two-thirds in each one, separately, not combined."

Xavier counted. Twenty senators, so two-thirds was fourteen, and they had fourteen, exactly, not one vote to spare. The House had thirty members, so two-thirds was twenty, and the House had passed it nineteen to eleven. He wrote the numbers on the card, crossed out nothing, and looked at the gap. One vote. Willy was a House member. Willy had voted yes already, so that wasn't it. He pulled the class list from his binder and went name by name, chair scraping on the floor, until he found the boy who had missed the Tuesday session for a dentist appointment.

The override vote was scheduled for Thursday, in the library again. Xavier spent Wednesday at the table by the periodicals, drafting a one-page summary of the health report for the boy who had been absent, and Athena proofread it and cut two sentences she called editorializing. Willy practiced arguing the counterpoint against himself out loud, playing both sides, so he could answer the plumbing objection if it came up again. It did come up. The boy with the dentist appointment read the summary during the debate, folded it into quarters, and raised his hand when Mr. Nkosi called the question.

The Senate voted first: fourteen to six, the same as before, nobody switching. Then the House, and Mr. Nkosi counted out loud, and it came to twenty to ten. Willy hit the table with his palm, not hard, just once, and the woman at the next carrel looked over the top of her glasses.

Mr. Nkosi took out the stamp. He pressed it onto the last page, and the word ASSENT came out slightly crooked, half on the paper and half on the wood. He handed the bill back to Xavier and said the session was adjourned and the room closed at six. Outside the window the parking lot lights had come on, and Athena was already photographing the stamped page with her phone.

"Next year," she said, "we do it with the real numbers. Real House, real Senate, all four hundred and thirty-five."

"Count me in for counting," Willy said, zipping his bag. Xavier folded the bill along the stamp line and put it in his binder between the health report and the class list, where the one vote's name was still circled in blue ink.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Robert Cialdini's 1976 study found that students wore more university clothing after their football team won and said 'we' more when describing wins than losses.
story:
The corner booth at Gino's had the best view of the big screen, and Brooke's father had claimed it forty minutes before kickoff, which meant the whole family was wedged around the table with Tanner and Gurshaan squeezed in at the end. The restaurant was loud in the way Brooke liked, everyone's attention pooled on the same glowing rectangle, waitresses weaving between chairs with trays held high. Ms. Rajapakse from next door had come along because her television was broken, and she kept asking which player was which, and Gurshaan kept patiently pointing, "That's the quarterback, that one," as though she were five instead of seventy.

What Brooke wanted, concretely, was for her father to see that she understood the game. Not just the rules, which she'd memorized years ago, but the wanting of it, the way he and Tanner stood up at the same moments and sat down at the same moments like one creature with four legs. She had a theory about that, actually, something she'd found in a psychology book while researching a paper for Ms. Rajapakse's class last spring, and she'd been waiting weeks for a chance to use it.

The fourth quarter was tight, three points apart, and when the receiver broke free down the sideline the whole restaurant rose. Brooke rose too. The pass fell incomplete, and her father groaned and dropped back into the booth, and Tanner said, "We should have run it up the middle," and Gurshaan said, "We'll get it back next drive." Brooke filed that away. She was starting to notice something.

With two minutes left the quarterback scrambled, bought time with his feet, and found the tight end in the back of the end zone. Tanner was on his chair. Gurshaan was pounding the table hard enough to rattle the water glasses. "We won," Tanner shouted, arms out, turning to the room as if to collect congratulations, "we won, we won." He had never played a down of football in his life. He had a doctor's note that got him out of gym.

Brooke waited for the noise to thin out, then said, "You know there was this study, 1976, by a guy named Robert Cialdini. He found that students wore more of their university's clothing after the football team won. And when they described a win, they said 'we.' When they described a loss, they didn't. They said 'they.'" She kept her voice level, the way you do when you're not accusing anyone, just reporting.

Tanner looked at her over the rim of his soda. "So?"

"So you've been saying 'we' all night, and you've never touched a football." She hadn't meant it to come out sharp, but there it was.

Gurshaan leaned in, interested, which was the reaction Brooke had wanted. Tanner's face went through something metamorphic, pride reshaping itself into defense and back again. "It's my school," he said finally. "I go there. Am I not allowed to feel it?"

"That's the thing," Brooke said. "I don't actually think you're wrong." And she found she meant it, which surprised her. She'd walked in thinking the "we" thing was a fraud, an easy borrowing of glory, a travesty of real belonging, the kind of thing you'd want to expose. But sitting here, watching her father hug the neighbor whose television was broken, watching Gurshaan text his cousin in another city the same three words Tanner had shouted, it didn't look like fraud. It looked like the games enfranchised people who never got on the field, gave them a vote in something, and the "we" was the ballot.

She tried to say some of that out loud. "Like, Cialdini's thing could mean people are just basking, taking credit for stuff they didn't do. That's one reading. But it could also mean the team actually belongs to everybody who watches, and the language is just catching up to that." She pushed a fry around her plate. "I can't tell which one it is. Honestly, I think both might be true at once, and I don't know how that works yet."

Tanner considered her for a long moment, then shrugged and stole one of her fries, which was his way of accepting a draw. Ms. Rajapakse raised her glass of lemonade and said, "To the we," and everyone at the table touched their cups to it, even Brooke, even as she kept turning the question over, unresolved, like a coin she hadn't stopped flipping. On the screen the coaches were shaking hands, and the replay started again from the snap.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: An equilibrium is dynamic: the forward and reverse reactions keep happening, but at equal rates, so the amounts of reactants and products stay constant.
story:
Jade had been staring at the same page of her chemistry review for twenty minutes when her mother called up that Edison was at the door, holding his textbook like a plate of food he wasn't sure he wanted. She let him in. They spread their notes across the kitchen table, which had not been cleared since breakfast, and Edison immediately rearranged everything into two suspiciously neat piles.

"Question four," he said. "You heat the mixture and it turns blue instead of pink. Explain using Le Chatelier's principle." He tapped the paper. "I wrote that the heat makes the reaction stop being balanced and start over in the other direction. Like a reset."

Jade had written something similar the night before, and something about it had been bothering her since, the way a word you've spelled wrong keeps looking almost right. She turned her notebook so he could see. She'd drawn two arrows, one on top of the other, pointing opposite ways. Under them she'd written a question mark and, in smaller letters, "but then nothing is happening?" which her teacher, Mr. Lin, had circled in red without comment. The circling without comment felt like a verdict. Or, she thought, possibly like an acquittal she hadn't earned yet.

"Here's my problem," she said. "If heating it shifts everything to products, then at some point the amounts stop changing. Mr. Lin said the solution sits there pink or blue for hours. So either the reaction finished, or it's pretending to be finished, and I don't know which one the exam wants."

Edison was famously garrulous in the hallways, where his running commentary on everyone's lockers had made him minorly celebrated, but over schoolwork he went quiet and slow, which was one of the reasons Jade studied with him. He frowned at her arrows. "Both arrows at once? That can't be right. A reaction can't go two directions."

"Why not? People can."

She was thinking of the café on Delancey Street, where she'd sat for three hours last Saturday with one tea. The room had been full when she arrived and full when she left, and the whole time there had been a steady shuffle at the door, people leaving with cups, people coming in from the cold, a line at the register that never got shorter or longer. She'd assumed, at first, that it was the same crowd. Then she'd noticed a man in a yellow coat go out and come back, twice, apparently unable to decide about the rain. The door kept moving. The room stayed the same.

"Okay," she said slowly, pulling a fresh sheet toward her. "The café. Say the reactants are people outside and the products are people inside. All afternoon the same number of people are sitting at the tables, right? Constant. But it's not because nobody moves. People keep going in and people keep coming out. Same number inside the whole time because the going-in and the coming-out happen at equal rates. Nothing's frozen. It just looks frozen if you only count heads."

Edison looked at the café doodle she was sketching, arrows through a door, little cups on little tables. "So when Mr. Lin says equilibrium, he doesn't mean the reaction stopped."

"An equilibrium is dynamic," Jade said, copying the phrase off her own arrows. "The forward and reverse reactions keep happening, but at equal rates, so the amounts of reactants and products stay constant." She underlined the last four words, then wished she hadn't, because it looked like studying, and this had begun to feel like something she'd actually figured out. She drew a counter above the café door and started making tally marks going in and coming out, matched pairs, while Edison held the pencil steady against the page for her.

"Then the heating question is easy," he said. "Heat it, and one direction slows down or speeds up, so the numbers drift until they match again. New balance, new color. Blue instead of pink."

"Maybe," Jade said. "That's the part I can't prove from a café." She could feel the shape of the idea and the hole in it at the same time. The shop told her that constant amounts could hide constant motion; it did not tell her why temperature would tilt the balance, or in which direction, and she wasn't going to pretend it did. She wrote "why heat? which way?" beside the tallies and boxed it for Mr. Lin, who was coming by anyway at six to return her mother's casserole dish.

When the doorbell rang, Edison hid the doodle under his neat piles, too late. Mr. Lin set the dish on the counter, looked at the page of arrows and tally marks and café tables, and raised one eyebrow at Jade in a way that seemed to presage either detention or a decent grade. He put his finger on her boxed question and read it aloud. "Good question," he said. "Which way do you think?"

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: The US Fair Labor Standards Act took effect on October 24, 1938, setting the first federal minimum wage at 25 cents an hour and a maximum workweek of 44 hours.
story:
The kitchen smelled of scorched butter and dish steam when Zoey clocked in, and the first thing she heard was Leane's voice, sharp over the hiss of the fryer. Leane was nineteen, a part-timer on the closing shift, and she was waving her schedule at the sous chef like a summons from a magistrate. Fourteen hours had been cut from her week, which meant her rent money had been cut too, and no one would tell her why. "Ask Ms. Hamdan," the sous chef kept saying, and Ms. Hamdan, who owned the place and had hired Zoey on a Tuesday because she liked Zoey's mother, kept not being in the building.

Zoey scraped the grill and thought about her own hours, which were fine, actually. Ms. Hamdan let her leave early on nights before exams and never scheduled her past eleven on school days. That kindness sat in Zoey's chest like a debt, and when Leane cornered her by the walk-in cooler, Zoey heard herself start to equivocate. "I mean, she's probably dealing with the food costs," she said, then, "I'm sure it's not personal," then, quieter, "I don't really know what happened." Leane looked at her the way you look at a locked door.

What happened, as it turned out, was on the corkboard by the time clock, half hidden under a health inspection notice. It was a printed memo from a regional restaurant association, addressed to all operators, warning about "outside organizers" and describing union certification as a threat to small businesses. Zoey had passed that corkboard a hundred times without reading anything on it. Now she read it twice, and a sentence about "unnecessary interference with scheduling flexibility" snagged on the thought of her exam nights. Flexibility was the exact word Ms. Hamdan used, warmly, whenever anyone asked about overtime.

That afternoon, in the dry storage room with her phone, Zoey looked it up herself, because she wanted to know where the rules she'd heard about actually came from. The screen glowed against the sacks of rice. The Fair Labor Standards Act, she read, took effect on October 24, 1938, and it set the first federal minimum wage at 25 cents an hour. It also set a maximum workweek of 44 hours. She sat with that for a moment. Twenty-five cents, in 1938. Forty-four hours, as a ceiling, not a floor. Somebody had drawn those lines once, from nothing, and every paycheck she'd ever gotten had been shaped inside them without her knowing.

She texted Cassandre from the milk cooler, where the humming drowned out everything.

"did you know there was literally a FIRST federal minimum wage. 25 cents. 1938."

Cassandre replied in a burst: "25 CENTS?? Leane should print that out and tape it to her timesheet. also the max workweek was 44 hours back then, which is wild, because dad does 60 at the warehouse and nobody says anything." Then: "wait are you getting union pamphlets at work? Leane DMed me. she wants to know if you'll sign a card."

Zoey typed and deleted three answers. The cooler dripped somewhere behind her, a slow cold percussion. She could sign, and Leane would have one more name toward the number the law required, and Ms. Hamdan might learn who had signed and might stop saying warmly, flexibly, nothing at all. Or she could not sign, and keep her easy hours, and keep her debt paid in the currency of silence. Both felt like answers someone braver would find obvious.

She found Leane by the dish pit and told her the thing she'd found, awkwardly, like offering half a sandwich. "The first federal minimum was 25 cents an hour. October 24, 1938. And the max workweek back then was 44 hours." Leane's hands kept moving in the grey water. "Twenty-five cents," she repeated, and laughed, a short sound with no floor under it. "They fought over twenty-five cents. Like, there were people who thought even that would ruin everything." She pulled a card from her apron pocket, soft at the corners from being carried. It was the same shape as the order slips, and somehow that made it look more official, not less.

Zoey signed it with the pen tied to the prep station on a length of twine, and Leane slid the card away without ceremony, the way you'd pocket a tip. For the rest of the shift Zoey waited for the sky to fall and noticed instead how the kitchen was a hundred small negotiations she'd never seen: the cook who traded Saturdays for a flat of tomatoes from his cousin's farm, the dishwasher who'd asked, as a group, for the broken floor mat to be replaced and got it in a week. It wasn't a union. It was something older and blurrier, people deciding together what they'd accept. Whether the card in Leane's pocket was that, or the beginning of a fight that would close the restaurant and take everyone's hours, including hers, Zoey could not have said, and she was tired of pretending she could.

Ms. Hamdan came in at close, hair damp from the rain, carrying a box of invoices. She stopped at the corkboard, took down the restaurant association's memo, folded it once, and put it in her coat pocket. Then she pinned something in its place, a little off-center, and went to the office without a word. Zoey wiped down the flat-top and watched the paper settle under the push-pin: a notice about a representation vote, with a date, and beneath the printed signature line of the organizer, a second signature, handwritten, small and slanted, that she'd seen before on her own hiring paperwork. Leane came out of the dish pit with wet hands and read it, and read it again, and turned to Zoey with the steam rising behind her. "She signed first," Leane said. "The owner signed first."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: According to the CDC, wearing a seat belt reduces serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half.
story:
The car was parked at the curb in front of Mr. Grant's house, a grey sedan with a magnetic sign on the door that read GRANT SAFE DRIVING in letters Cameron found faintly grandiose for a suburban street where the most dramatic event of the summer had been a fallen birch. Cameron had been ascribing his nervousness to the car itself, the unfamiliar pedals and the mirror he would have to trust more than his own neck, but standing at the curb he understood the nervousness was really about the fact that his mother was watching from the porch and he wanted, more than almost anything, not to embarrass himself in front of her.

"You're Cameron," Mr. Grant said. It wasn't a question. He was a wide man in a short-sleeved shirt, and he carried a clipboard the way a referee carries a whistle, as if penalties were always imminent. "Before you touch anything, tell me what you notice about the car."

Cameron walked around it once. Tires fine, no dents, the passenger side mirror angled wrong for him. Then he got in, adjusted the seat, gripped the wheel at ten and two the way the booklet said, and reached for the ignition.

"Stop."

Mr. Grant wasn't even looking at him. He was looking at the seat belt, still retracted against the door pillar.

"Last week I had a girl," Mr. Grant said, taking the clipboard onto his lap, "sat right there where you're sitting, started the engine, put it in gear. In the driveway. I made her get out and we sat on my porch for the whole hour. Her mother paid for a lesson she didn't drive in."

"Because of the belt?"

"Tell me why."

Cameron had read the state manual twice, but this wasn't in it, or not in the part he'd memorized. He thought about the girl sitting on the porch, her hour evaporating, and about what a person would have to believe to refuse to move a car one foot for a missing belt. "Because it's the rule," he tried.

"Rules I could ascribe to bureaucracy," Mr. Grant said. "The CDC says a seat belt cuts serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half. Half. From one piece of webbing." He let that sit. "Now tell me why."

Cameron pulled the belt across his chest and clicked it, and the click was louder than he expected. He was thinking that half was a strange number, enormous and small at once, and that if you believed it, the belt wasn't a rule at all, it was arithmetic. "Because if it's half," he said slowly, "then not wearing it is the one thing in the car you control completely. The road's random. This isn't."

Mr. Grant grunted, which Cameron was beginning to suspect was his highest form of praise. "Put it in drive. Foot on the brake first. We're going to the end of the street and back, and you're going to tell me what you see."

The car crept forward. Cameron had imagined his first drive as a leap into traffic, something cinematic, but it was more like a proof in geometry class, where each small move followed from the last one. He liked proofs. There was a lemma in the unit they'd just finished, a little helper statement you proved on the way to the real theorem, too small to be the point but impossible to skip. The belt was like that, he decided. Not the theorem of driving, just the thing you had to establish first.

At the stop sign he braked too hard and the belt caught his chest, and instead of being annoyed he noticed it, the way it held him without his asking. He eased around the corner. Matthieu's house went by on the left, and Alden was out front waxing his bike, and both of them watched the grey sedan the way people watch a funeral, and Cameron lifted two fingers off the wheel at them, and Alden laughed so hard he dropped his rag.

"Mirrors," Mr. Grant said. "Every eight seconds. What's behind you?"

Cameron checked. Nothing but the long empty street and his mother, small now on the porch, one hand raised. He had spent an hour that morning arguing with her about whether a driving instructor was necessary, whether he could just learn from his father, whether the whole thing was an expensive ritual. He had been so certain. Now, moving at fifteen miles an hour with the belt pressed warm against his collarbone, he wasn't sure the certainty had been about the lesson at all. Maybe it had been about wanting to be the kind of person who didn't need one, and maybe those were different questions, and maybe he'd figure out which one mattered by the end of the summer, or maybe he wouldn't.

"Again," Mr. Grant said. "End of the street and back. And Cameron, this time, tell me what you notice before I ask."

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: In the United States, courts generally will not enforce a liability waiver that tries to excuse gross negligence or intentional misconduct, even if the person signed it.
story:
The branch smelled of carpet cleaner and cooled coffee, and the crepuscular light through the tall windows made everything look like a photograph taken an hour before closing. Isabella took a number from the dispenser, sat beside her mother, and watched the digits climb toward hers on the screen. She had brought her passport, her acceptance letter, and ninety-three dollars in a Ziploc bag, because the community college required direct deposit for work-study pay and her mother had decided that today, of all days, was the day to make her an adult.

When her number came up, the officer who waved her over introduced himself as Mr. Lewandowski and slid a stack of paperwork across the desk with the ceremony of a man presenting a treaty. "This one's the signature card," he said. "This one covers the terms and conditions of the account. Initial here, here, and here." Isabella picked up the chained pen and did not initial. She read. The first page alone contained the words liability, consent, disclosure, and indemnify, and she read the paragraph containing indemnify three times before admitting to herself that she did not know what it meant and would be signing it anyway.

Behind her, Jaylynn had come along for the ride and was narrating in a low voice. "This bank is basically a theocracy," she whispered, gesturing at the framed certificates on the wall. "Fine print is scripture, Mr. Lewandowski is the high priest, and you are about to convert." Their history teacher had used the word that week about a government they were studying, and Jaylynn had been deploying it everywhere since, at lunch, in the parking lot, now at the teller windows. Isabella shushed her, but she was smiling, and Mr. Lewandowski, who had overheard, cleared his throat in a way that did not quite presage trouble, more like light rain.

"I can explain any of it," he said. "Most people don't ask."

"What's the bank still responsible for," Isabella asked, "if I sign all this? Like, what can't you make me waive?"

Mr. Lewandowski tilted his hand back and forth. "Some things you can't sign away. Fraud, for one. But your questions will answer faster if you read the disclosures. I'm required to give them to you, and you're required to receive them, and beyond that we're all just people in a carpeted room."

While he photocopied her passport, her mind drifted to the other signature waiting in her life, the climbing gym waiver. She and Jaylynn had signed up for the introductory belay course on Saturday, and last night her father had read the form at the kitchen table, pen hovering, and finally asked her whether she understood what she was agreeing to. She had said yes. She had not entirely been telling the truth, and the small dishonesty had sat with her through dinner like a stone in a shoe.

The gym's front desk was where Loan worked, Saturdays only, and Isabella had texted her the question rather than answer it herself. Loan's reply had come in three bubbles. "lol everyone freaks out about that form." Then: "my manager says courts generally won't enforce a waiver that tries to excuse gross negligence or intentional misconduct, even if the person signed it." Then a shrugging emoji. Isabella had read the middle message several times, not because it comforted her exactly, but because it redrew the whole page. The waiver was not a wall; it was a wall with a gate in it. She could not have said where the gate opened or who decided, only that it existed, and that the gym could not make her sign away everything no matter how many lines she initialed.

At the desk, Mr. Lewandowski returned with her passport and a folder. "Account's open once you sign," he said. "Or you can take the forms home. There's no penalty for reading them overnight."

Her mother shifted in the chair. "We drove forty minutes."

"We did," Isabella said. She looked at the signature line, then at the paragraph about electronic transfers, then at Jaylynn, who mouthed convert. She thought of her father at the kitchen table, pen hovering, wanting her to understand, and of Loan's text, which had come from a manager and therefore might itself be wrong, a secondhand fact she had chosen to trust because it was easier than reading. She was honest enough with herself to notice that. She signed her name twice, in cursive the way she had practiced in fourth grade, and slid the folder back across the desk.

Outside, the streetlights were coming on and the air had the cool edge that comes after a hot day. Jaylynn bumped her shoulder. "So Saturday you're basically signing another one of those."

"Basically," Isabella said. "Except this time I already know the form can't cover everything."

"Everything like what?"

She zipped the Ziploc bag, empty now, into her backpack. "Ask me after I read it again."

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Robert Millikan measured the charge of the electron by using the electric field between two horizontal charged plates to hold tiny charged oil drops still against gravity.
story:
The lab smelled of rubbing alcohol and the faint scorched tang of a burner someone had left on too long, and Alexander sat with his quiz face down in front of him because turning it over felt like opening a door into a room he already knew was destitute of anything good. Forty-eight percent. Ms. Vogel had written it in red at the top, and beside question four, the one about the electric field between two parallel plates, she had drawn a single bracket and the word "direction?"

"He put the arrow pointing down," Angelique said, leaning over from the next stool without shame. "For a positive test charge. Between the plates."

"You're supposed to be helping me, not narrating my funeral," Alexander said.

Kiana spun her stool toward them both. She had done the reading, obviously; she always had, the way some people always had umbrellas. "It's not even hard," she said, and then, because she was kind underneath the bluntness, she pulled her notebook around and started sketching. Two horizontal lines, a plus sign on the top plate, a minus on the bottom. "The field goes from positive to negative. Then the strength is just the voltage divided by the distance. Volts per metre."

Alexander copied the diagram, hating how simple it looked once it was drawn, hating that he had spent twenty minutes on the quiz rearranging the same three variables like a man moving furniture in a dark room. "So if it's twelve volts and the plates are, what, three centimetres apart."

"Zero point zero three metres," Kiana said. "Units. Always units."

"Four hundred volts per metre," he said, and something in his chest shifted, not triumph exactly, more like the click of a lock that had been refusing the key out of pure spite.

Ms. Vogel came down the row and set a small photocopied page beside his quiz. It was a picture of a brass cylinder in a glass case, plates visible inside it, a plaque below. "Extra credit," she said. "Tell me whose apparatus this is and what he did with it. You've seen it before, I think."

He had. The recognition arrived before the memory did, the way thunder sometimes beats its own storm. A science museum, years ago, a Saturday when his father still drove him places. His father had stopped at a replica in a glass case and said, look at this, this is how they caught the electron, and Alexander, maybe nine, had cared more about the vending machine on the next floor. But he remembered the shape now, and he remembered the words on the plaque, because he had read them twice while his father found his glasses.

"That's Millikan," he said, and then, carefully, because the facts had to be laid down in the right order like the plates themselves, "Robert Millikan measured the charge of the electron. He used the electric field between two horizontal charged plates to hold tiny charged oil drops still against gravity."

"Still," Ms. Vogel repeated, tapping the picture. "What does still tell you?"

Alexander looked at his diagram, the arrow he had drawn wrong, and then at the photograph, where the two horizontal plates sat one above the other like a ceiling and a floor. If a drop hung motionless, the field pushing up and gravity pulling down, then the forces balanced, and that meant you could know one by knowing the other. "The forces cancel," he said slowly. "The field has to be exactly strong enough. So the equation isn't just a formula, it's, like, a scale."

"Like a scale," Ms. Vogel said, and moved on down the row.

Angelique was watching him with an expression that did not portend anything gentle. "You're actually going to do the extra credit."

"My dad took me to that museum," Alexander said. He hadn't meant to say it; it came out the way the arithmetic had, one thing forcing the next. "I didn't pay attention. He paid attention. He read every plaque." There was a Saturday schedule once, and then there wasn't, and the vending machine on the next floor had been more interesting than the brass cylinder, and none of that could be fixed by four hundred volts per metre.

Kiana slid the photocopy closer and smoothed its curled corner. "Then write it up," she said. "You have until Friday."

He turned his quiz over and began, in the margin of the failure, to draw the plates again: positive on top, negative below, the field running down between them like rain that fell in perfectly straight lines. Somewhere in a glass case, a drop of oil hung still, held up and held down at once, and Alexander copied the diagram a second time, pressing hard enough that the pencil bit through the page.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut's dual process model describes grieving people as moving back and forth between facing the loss and getting on with rebuilding daily life, rather than moving in one direction.
story:
The casseroles had started arriving before the funeral was over, so by the time Benjamin walked into his grandmother's kitchen that afternoon, the counter was a wall of foil and Tupperware, and his aunts moved among the dishes like air traffic controllers. His grandfather had died eight days ago. Benjamin had cried at the service, held his mother's hand, carried a corner of the casket with his older cousin, and now he was standing in the pantry doorway holding a bag of rolls he'd been told to bring out, watching everyone eat.

He put the rolls down and went to find the folding chairs in the garage. Halfway there, his cousin's husband was telling the story about the time Grandpa drove thirty miles with the parking brake on, smoke pouring off the wheels, refusing to stop because he "wasn't paying to replace the shoes twice." Benjamin laughed before he could stop himself, a real laugh, loud in the hallway, and then the guilt arrived so fast it felt physical, like swallowing something the wrong way. He stood there with his hand over his mouth.

His Uncle Theo noticed. Theo was the quiet one, the one who fixed things at gatherings, and he didn't say anything right away, just carried two chairs past Benjamin and set them in the living room, then came back. "Eight days," he said, not quite a question.

"I laughed," Benjamin said. "The parking brake story."

"Your grandfather told me that story forty times and I laughed every single time." Theo rubbed the back of his neck. "After your Nana died, I felt like I was going crazy. Someone would mention her and I'd fall apart, and an hour later I'd be watching football and actually enjoying it. Then I'd feel like a traitor. A cousin of mine finally told me there was a name for it, some researchers, Stroebe and Schut. Called it the dual process model." He picked up another chair. "I'm not explaining it. You can look it up. But you're allowed to laugh at the parking brake."

Benjamin found the chairs, found his phone, and stood in the cold garage where the smell of motor oil still hung the way it had when Grandpa spent Saturdays out here. He read that grieving people move back and forth between facing the loss and getting on with rebuilding daily life, rather than moving in one direction, and that the moving back and forth itself was the normal thing, not a failure of it. He read it twice. He didn't feel better exactly, but he felt like he'd been handed a map of terrain he'd already been stumbling across in the dark.

Inside, he started watching for it, and once he saw it, he couldn't stop seeing it. His mother sat at the table telling a story about her father's terrible handwriting, tears sliding down her face, and twenty minutes later she was out by the grill arguing with his uncle about whether to use the good sausages. His little cousin went from sobbing on the stairs to being completely captivated by a video game, then sobbed again at bedtime when she remembered the recliner was empty. Nobody moved through anything in one direction. They swung out and came back, out and back, like the porch swing Grandpa had hung the summer before Benjamin was born.

In the study, his father and Aunt Ruth were sorting papers, and Aunt Ruth, dour even on holidays, held up a yellowed document with a look of actual delight. "It's an affidavit," she said. "From 1974. He swore out a statement about the neighbor's fence. Two pages. He kept two pages about a fence for fifty years." They laughed until Aunt Ruth had to sit down, and then she was abruptly crying, one hand flat on the affidavit, and nobody rushed her, and nobody told her to stop either.

Campbell texted him around seven, asking if he was okay, and Kaitlynn sent a photo of the three of them from last summer at the lake, and Benjamin wrote back that he was okay, that the house was full of food and aunts and stories, and that he'd see them Monday. He hesitated before sending it, then added, honestly, some of it was even good. He meant it. The grief was still there, waiting for him in the recliner and in the smell of the garage, but so was the parking brake story, and the swing, and the ridiculous fence affidavit, which Aunt Ruth had decided to frame.

Late that evening, after most of the family had gone or fallen asleep in chairs, Benjamin went out to the porch. The swing was still up, its chain slightly rusted. He sat down and pushed off with his heel, once, and let it carry him out and back, out and back, until it slowed on its own. From inside, faintly, he could hear his mother laughing at something on the kitchen phone, and he sat there listening, still swinging.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: The 'guidance hypothesis' from motor learning research holds that feedback after every single attempt can make learners dependent on it, so less frequent feedback often helps retention.
story:
Robert arrived at the diamond early, before the eleven-year-olds, and dragged the bucket of balls to the stretch of grass between second base and the mound. He had agreed to run Thursday practices because Mr. Müller, who coached the league's youngest team, had twisted a knee and could no longer demonstrate anything. Robert was eighteen and had played shortstop for six years, which made him, in the coach's opinion, qualified. The kids could hit, more or less. What they could not do was throw to each other. A routine toss from second to first went sailing into the fence, or died in the dirt five feet short of the bag, and every game they lost, they lost that way.

At first Robert stood behind them and said something after every throw. Elbow up. Step toward the target. Follow through. The kids obeyed, one correction at a time, and practice looked tidy. But when the scrimmages started, and Robert stood back by the fence where his voice could not reach them, the throws fell apart as if the whole team had forgotten the skill overnight. He watched a boy named Danny sail one over the first baseman's head and then look toward the fence, waiting for the sentence that would tell him what he had done.

Robert complained about it that Friday to Yuna, who was reading motor learning articles for a college course she had talked her way into early. "It has a name," she said, not looking up. "The guidance hypothesis." She slid her laptop across the table. "Feedback after every single attempt can make learners dependent on it. Less frequent feedback often helps retention." Robert read the paragraph twice, then a second study, then sat for a while with his chin in his hand.

He was honest enough with himself to admit that the corrections had felt good to give. Each one was a small proof that he knew something. And there was a competing idea in him, older and more stubborn: that a coach who says nothing looks lazy, that silence reads as indifference, that the parents on the bleachers would vilify him if their children threw balls into the parking lot while he stood and watched. He weighed that fear against the memory of Danny's face, turned hopefully toward the fence, and decided the fear was worth less.

On Thursday he set up the drill differently. He marked a square in the grass with cones, ten feet to a side, and paired the kids off. Partner throwing, one ball each pair, and the goal was simply to keep the ball inside the square for thirty throws. He explained the target once. Then he told them he was going to time the innings and would say nothing unless they asked. "Nothing?" Celina's little brother asked, scandalized. "You're the coach." Robert said that was the drill, and walked to the mound, where he sat on the rubber with a stopwatch and tried to look like a man with a plan rather than a man doing nothing.

The first ten throws were ugly. A ball skipped off Celina's brother's shin and he laughed; a ball nearly took off a hat. Robert bit down on every correction that rose in him. Around the fifteenth throw, the kids started talking to each other instead of to him. "You're dropping your arm," one said. "Try standing sideways," said another, in the tone of a boy reciting a bromide he had heard from his grandfather, and Robert nearly laughed, because the bromide actually worked. The throws began to arrive flat and fast and inside the square.

At the scrimmage the following Saturday, Mr. Müller stood beside Robert at the fence with his cane. Second baseman to first, a one-hop bullet, an out. The next one, a line drive right into the glove, no bounce at all. Mr. Müller watched a long time before he spoke. "I used to correct every single pass," he said, and there was something almost metamorphic in his voice, the sound of a man rearranging twenty years of coaching in a single afternoon. "Every one. And they always fell apart in games."

"It's not your fault," Robert said. "I did the same thing for two weeks."

"That's worse," Mr. Müller said, but he was smiling. Out at second base, Danny fielded a ground ball, planted his feet, and threw without once looking toward the fence. The first baseman caught it clean and held the ball up so everyone could see.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: In Ontario, when a fixed-term lease ends, the tenant does not have to sign a new one; the tenancy continues month to month automatically on the same terms.
story:
Sebastian stood in the produce section with two leases folded in his back pocket and a shopping list his mother had texted him, and he could not decide between the bagged spinach and the bunch, which was somehow easier than deciding between the apartments. Saad had texted him a photo of a unit on Caldwell Street, five hundred square feet, utilities extra. Lynden's building was farther from campus but heat and water were included, and the lease said so in a font small enough to seem embarrassed of itself. Sebastian put the bunch of spinach in the cart because his mother had written "the good kind," which he took to mean that one.

He had done the math twice at the kitchen table last night and gotten two different answers. The Caldwell unit was forty dollars cheaper in rent, but Saad's cousin who lived there said hydro ran high in winter, maybe eighty, maybe a hundred and twenty, a range so wide it felt like weather forecasting. Lynden's place bundled everything except internet and parking. Sebastian had built a spreadsheet with a column for best case and a column for worst case, and the two apartments traded places depending on which column he believed, which seemed like a bad property for a spreadsheet to have.

Mr. Ito was at the deli counter, third in line, and Sebastian got in behind him with his number tag. Mr. Ito had taught him grade eleven functions and now, in retirement, shopped on Wednesday afternoons with a list written on the back of an envelope. He glanced at Sebastian's cart, at the spinach, and said, "Your mother sent you. I can tell. You shop like someone with instructions."

"She's working doubles," Sebastian said. "And I'm moving out, so she's training me."

"Where to?" Mr. Ito asked, and Sebastian pulled the folded pages from his pocket and held them both out like a bad hand of cards. Mr. Ito read with his glasses pushed up on his forehead, which meant he was squinting, which meant he was concentrating. He tapped the Caldwell lease. "This one ends next August," he said. "They'll want you to sign another year."

"I know. That's the plan, though. Second year too."

Mr. Ito handed the pages back and turned toward the counter as his number came up. "When a fixed-term lease ends in Ontario," he said, "you don't have to sign a new one. The tenancy continues month to month automatically, on the same terms." He ordered a half kilogram of smoked turkey, thin sliced, and while the slicer ran he said nothing else, and Sebastian stood there holding the two leases with his mouth slightly open, feeling the ground shift under a plan he had thought was solid.

At the checkout, Sebastian laid out the problem for the cashier, who was seventeen at most and clearly regretting eye contact. Lynden appeared two lanes over, waving, and came across with a basket of instant noodles and a jar of peanut butter. "You decide yet?" Lynden asked. "Because my landlord already sent me the renewal form for after August. He made it sound like it was required. Like paperwork you have to do."

"He can ask," Sebastian said, and even as he said it he was circumspect about how far to push, because a landlord who wanted a year committed might not love a tenant who knew he didn't have to give one. "You don't have to sign it. It just goes month to month. Same terms." Lynden stared at him, and Sebastian added, "Mr. Ito. Deli counter." Lynden pulled out his phone and started typing a message to his landlord, then stopped halfway and looked up. "Wait, is that actually true, or is it deli-counter true?"

"That's the thing," Sebastian said. "I'm going to look it up before you send anything." He paid for the groceries, and the two of them stood by the carts by the doors, the automatic doors opening and closing on the cold, Sebastian doing the search on his phone while Lynden read over his shoulder. The tenant board page loaded slowly. Outside, an old man was struggling with a cart whose wheel had seized, and Lynden broke off from reading to go help him wrench it free, which took a while and involved kneeling in a puddle of slush.

The page came up. Sebastian read it once, then again, and the words matched what Mr. Ito had said in the deli line, exactly, no fine print taking it back. Month to month, same terms, automatic. He felt something between relief and vertigo, because it changed the math he'd been doing: if he took Caldwell, he wasn't locked into a second year he might not want, and the cheaper rent plus the ugly winter hydro might still win if he could leave when the program ended. But he still didn't know what hydro actually cost, and he still didn't know if he'd want to stay a second year, and no law in Ontario was going to tell him that. Lynden came back with wet knees and held out his hand for the phone.

"Read it to me," Lynden said. "The part about the same terms."

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: In We Now Know, published in 1997 after Soviet archives had partly opened, Gaddis placed much more responsibility on Stalin personally for the Cold War.
story:
Vanessa had spread the two books across her grandmother's kitchen table like evidence at a trial, which was more or less what they were. The first, a fat paperback from the school library, argued that the Cold War had been a shared failure, that both powers had stumbled into it through mutual fear. The second, newer and thinner, argued something sharper. She had checked them out after Ms. Gallagher told the class that historians disagreed about who was responsible, expecting the disagreement to run between two rival scholars. Instead she had found the same name on both spines. Gaddis.

"You're reading two books by the same man," her grandmother said, setting down a cup of tea that Vanessa hadn't asked for and didn't touch. "Is that allowed?"

"I don't know yet." Vanessa turned the older book over, then the newer one, as if the answer might be printed on the back. The newer one was called We Now Know, which had struck her as an odd title for a history. "He wrote the first one in the seventies, before I was born. The second one came out in 1997." She paused. "That's after the Soviet archives opened."

Her grandmother lowered herself into the chair across the table, moving the way she did now, carefully, one hand on the chair back. "And that matters?"

"It might." Vanessa opened We Now Know to the pages she had marked with a paper clip, because she had run out of bookmarks two nights ago. Somewhere in her bag was the essay prompt, and somewhere under the prompt was the question that had been circling her all week: how do you weigh one historian's word against his own earlier word? "In the newer book he puts a lot more of the responsibility on Stalin personally. Not on the Soviet system, not on both sides. On Stalin."

Santino had texted her twice about it, mostly to complain that the essay was unfair. two gaddises, he had written, which historian are we supposed to trust?? She hadn't answered, because the honest reply was that she didn't know, and she hated typing that. Alexandre, who read everything twice and annotated in pencil, had said only, check the dates, which she had already done, and which hadn't resolved anything. The dates told her when the man changed his mind. They didn't tell her whether the change was an improvement or a capitulation, whether the archives had genuinely transformed the evidence or merely given him cover for a position he had wanted all along.

She pulled a legal pad toward her and began to transcribe the passages that seemed to matter, the older book's careful, circumspect language about mutual misperception, the newer book's blunter claims. The grandmother's kitchen was quiet except for the tick of the clock over the doorway and, outside, a cardinal landing on the feeder and leaving again. Writing out the sentences by hand slowed her down in a way she liked. On the page, the older Gaddis sounded like a man hedging his bets. The newer one sounded like a man who had seen something.

"But he'd seen more," she said aloud.

"Who?"

"Gaddis. In 1997 he could read things he couldn't read in the seventies. Soviet documents." Vanessa tapped the legal pad. "So is it that he got smarter, or just luckier? And if a historian can change his mind that much, what does that do to the whole idea of trusting historians?"

Her grandmother considered this while stirring her tea, though Vanessa was fairly sure there was nothing left to stir. "Your grandfather changed his mind about the church when he was sixty. Nobody thought that made him untrustworthy. Some people thought it made him honest."

Vanessa wrote that down too, then felt slightly ridiculous about it and kept it anyway. She worked through the afternoon, testing each of the older book's claims against what the newer one said the documents showed, and the trouble was that she could not check the documents herself. She was sixteen, in her grandmother's kitchen, three weeks from the start of junior year. She had two books and a prompt and the memory of Ms. Gallagher saying, evidence first, then your reading of it, which Vanessa had at the time dismissed as a platitude and now suspected was the entire assignment.

The honest essay, she realized, would have to admit the hole in the middle of it. Gaddis had seen the archives; she had not. She could weigh the two books against each other, and she could say why the second one persuaded her more, the specificity of it, the way it named a person instead of a system. But she could not independently verify, and pretending otherwise would be exactly the kind of quiet dishonesty that made her stop trusting certain writers in the first place.

She started drafting near five o'clock, when the light through the kitchen window had gone the color of weak tea. The first paragraph came out stiff and she crossed it out. The second one began, The same historian, given twenty years and new evidence, reached a different conclusion, and that sentence she underlined twice. Santino texted again: figured it out yet?? She typed not exactly, then deleted it, then typed, sort of. He changes his mind and I change mine about him depending on which page I'm on. Then she set the phone face down on the table.

Her grandmother came back with two slices of bread and jam, sliding one plate toward Vanessa without comment. Vanessa ate with her left hand and kept writing with her right, and outside the cardinal returned to the feeder and stayed this time.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: A half cadence ends a phrase on the V chord, which sounds unfinished and makes the listener expect another phrase to follow.
story:
Maira's kitchen smelled of burnt toast and pencil shavings, and the piano against the far wall had been pushed there, Arianna suspected, only after her friend's parents gave up on anyone playing it. The assignment was due Monday: sixteen bars, a real melody, chord changes, standard notation. Mr. Nolan had said it in class the way he said everything, flat and unhurried, as though the difficulty were a rumor he refused to aggrandize. Most of the class had groaned. Arianna had written it in her notebook underlined twice, because it was the first assignment that asked for something she could not fake.

She had faked plenty. Four years of choir had taught her to follow the person beside her, and two semesters of theory had taught her which answers Mr. Nolan accepted. But melody was different. You could not borrow it, and you could not bluff it, and she had spent Wednesday and Thursday evenings at the school piano producing lines that collapsed by the fifth bar like wet paper.

"Play it again," Maira said, chin in her hand. Maira was loquacious about nearly everything, parties, the cashier at the corner store, the neighbor's dog, but she went quiet around music, which Arianna had always taken as a kind of respect.

Arianna played the eight bars she had. They were fine. That was the problem. They were four chords in a loop with a tune sitting on top, tidy and dead, and when she lifted her hands the sound just stopped, like a door closing on an empty room.

Kristopher came in through the back door without knocking, holding the guitar he carried everywhere the way other people carried phones. He set it against the counter, looked at her manuscript paper, and tapped bar eight with one finger. "It ends here?"

"That's the phrase," Arianna said. "Eight bars, then it repeats."

"Play it again and stop at eight. Don't do anything after."

She did. The last chord hung in the air, wrong in a way she couldn't name, like a sentence that stopped before the verb. Kristopher was grinning, which annoyed her, until she understood that the grin was not at her.

"You ended on five," he said. "The V chord. My cousin did the same thing and our teacher called it a half cadence. Ends the phrase on the V, sounds unfinished, makes the listener expect another phrase to follow."

"It sounds unfinished," Arianna repeated, slowly, because the words were rearranging something in her head.

"On purpose, though. It's a hook. You leave people leaning forward."

She looked at her paper. She had landed there by accident, chasing a note that seemed easiest to reach, and the accident had produced the one interesting thing in eight bars. That irritated her more than the dead loop had. She had wanted to build something and instead she had tripped into something, and she could not entirely tell whether the difference mattered.

Maira pulled a chair up beside her. "So don't fix it," she said. "Use it. Eight bars that stop on the V, then eight more that actually finish."

"Then the first half isn't a mistake anymore. It's a setup." Arianna wrote V under the last beat of bar eight and drew an arrow to bar nine. "But that means bars nine through sixteen have to earn it. They can't just repeat."

Kristopher picked up the guitar and played her melody back, doubling the rhythm, then halving it, then wandering off it entirely into something that was better and not hers. She stopped him with a hand on the neck of the guitar. "Mine," she said, and he laughed and handed it back to silence.

She worked for another hour. Maira made toast that came out right this time and buttered it without being asked, leaving the plate on the piano's flat edge where Arianna could reach it without looking up. The melody for bars nine to sixteen came in pieces, one interval at a time, and she wrote every note in her slow careful hand, stem directions checked, the notation itself a language she was still learning to speak at speed. Twice she erased a whole bar. Once she erased two.
