Somewhere past ten o'clock she finished a line that curved up through a chord she would not have chosen a week ago, and let it settle, at the very end, onto a chord that closed like a breath let out.

"Play the whole thing," Maira said.

Arianna played all sixteen bars through, the first phrase hanging open at bar eight the way she wanted it to, the second phrase answering. When she finished, nobody said anything. Kristopher was looking at the manuscript paper, at the arrow she had drawn, and she could see him deciding whether to say something.

"That's it," he said finally. "That's the assignment."

"It's one assignment," Arianna said, and started copying it onto a clean sheet, in ink this time, her hand steady on the first note.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: US employers withhold 6.2 percent of an employee's wages for Social Security tax, up to a yearly wage limit.
story:
Stella counted the bills twice in the employee bathroom, standing over the sink with the door locked, and both times the number came out wrong. Nine hours at eleven dollars an hour should have been ninety-nine dollars, minus a little for the state, but the check Ms. Ricci had handed her said $84.51, and the difference sat in Stella's pocket like a stone. She had worked Saturday and Sunday at the coffee shop, pulling shots and wiping down the pastry case while Ms. Ricci, who owned the place, watched the register the way other people watched weather. Fourteen dollars and forty-nine cents was not a fortune. It was, however, hers, or she had believed it was.

"That's not right," Corey said that evening, from the stool nearest the window, where he'd claimed a corner table with his turgid AP history textbook open to a chapter he clearly wasn't reading. He leaned over her pay stub, which Stella had flattened on the table between two mugs of the shop's cheapest drip. "You did nine hours. I watched you do nine hours. You brought me a defective croissant and everything."

"It wasn't defective. It was rustic." But she had already begun the arithmetic on a napkin, and the arithmetic was not on her side. She subtracted what she knew: state tax, which she'd looked up months ago when she'd first wanted this job, came to almost nothing at her income. Federal withholding, likewise, nearly zero. That left a line on the stub she'd never examined before, a deduction labeled with initials she'd seen her whole life on signs and never once thought about, taking a percentage that, when she worked it backward, came to six point two percent of her wages. Exactly.

"Maybe she's skimming," Corey said, dropping his voice the way people do when the accusation is worse for being quiet. "Small place, cash business, a sixteen-year-old who's not going to sue anybody."

Stella looked up at Ms. Ricci behind the counter, drawing a fern into the foam of a cappuccino with a steady wrist, and thought about how the woman had spent ten minutes on the phone that afternoon arguing with a supplier over the ethics of raising prices on regulars. The image didn't prove anything. Still, Stella had been enraptured by that same latte art during her interview, watching Ms. Ricci's hands, and she found she didn't want the woman to be a thief. Wanting something wasn't evidence either. She was starting to notice how many of her opinions were just preferences wearing costumes.

She texted Terrence, whose older brother had worked two summers at the garden center. Terrence texted back a photo of a pay stub from the brother's files, and there it was on his stub too, the same initials, the same six point two percent, deducted by a large company that had never met Ms. Ricci. Corey studied the photo, then slid it back across the table, and Stella could see him revising something in his face. "Okay," he said. "So not just her."

The next afternoon Stella brought her napkin math to the counter during the slow hour. "There's a line on my check," she said, and turned the stub toward Ms. Ricci. "Six point two percent. Every check, mine and Terrence's brother's too."

"Social Security," Ms. Ricci said, rinsing the steam wand. "It comes out of everyone's wages, up to a yearly wage limit. After that, it stops." She dried her hands and did not launch into anything further, only rang up the next customer, a woman who ordered a drink whose menu description was so elaborate it could have been a legal document.

Stella carried her mop bucket toward the back and stood for a moment beside the bags of coffee, adding the fact to the other facts. She still didn't know everything; whether the money would ever come back to her, in what form, after how many decades, was a question with no napkin big enough to hold it. But she knew she had been paid correctly, and that Corey had been wrong, and that she herself had been wrong before that, ready to believe a person was stealing from her because a number surprised her. She felt the strange, uneven satisfaction of owing someone a reparation she had no intention of making out loud, an apology folded up and kept.

Corey came in at closing to walk her home. He set his history book on the counter, and she noticed he'd actually gotten somewhere in it, his pen marks reaching the middle pages.

"For the record," he said, "I take back the skimming thing."

"Noted," Stella said, and untied her apron.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Many Orthodox churches, including the Russian Orthodox Church, celebrate Christmas on January 7 because they keep December 25 on the older Julian calendar.
story:
Katherine's grandmother had said it once, in the kitchen, while kneading dough for the pierogi: "We keep Christmas on December 25, but on the old Julian calendar, so it falls on January 7 for us." At the time Katherine had nodded and gone back to her phone. Now, standing at the door of the community hall with two boxes of ornaments, she wished she had asked more.

The hall smelled of wax and fried onions. Volunteers from the parish were dragging folding tables into a long line, and her mother was arguing with a man about where the tree should go, near the radiator or away from it. Katherine carried the boxes past them. Outside, the neighbors' Christmas was two weeks gone, their trees already at the curb, and here her family was stringing lights onto a spruce that had stood in a bucket of water in Mr. Khan's garage since the twenty-third, waiting.

"Nice tree," said Mr. Khan, holding the door open with his shoulder. He lived two houses down and had offered the garage space without being asked, which her mother still mentioned at dinner. "You know my nephew's wife is Russian Orthodox. Same thing. January 7." He said it the way he said most things, as a fact about the world, and went to help with the tables.

Katherine had invited Asher and Ayah on Tuesday, in the school parking lot, half by accident. Ayah had said yes immediately. Asher had laughed, not unkindly, and said, "A second Christmas? Do you get double presents?" She had not known what to say, and the not-knowing had bothered her for three days. She knew the date. She did not know how to hold the date up against his question without it sounding like a defense.

They arrived at six, stamping snow off their boots. Ayah brought a box of baklava from her aunt's shop, which she set down beside the pierogi as if it had always belonged there. Asher brought nothing but his posture, hands in pockets, taking in the icons propped on easels near the stage, the women in headscarves, the children racing between chairs. He looked, Katherine thought, like someone translating in his head.

"So it's Christmas," he said. "Like, actual Christmas."

"It's Christmas on December 25," Katherine said, "on the Julian calendar, which is the older one, so it comes out to January 7. That's why we're two weeks behind the neighbors." She heard her grandmother's cadence in it and was embarrassed by that, a little, the way you're embarrassed hearing your own voice on a recording.

"Huh." Asher watched a woman pin a kerchief onto a squirming girl. "I figured it was, like, a different holiday with the same name."

"No. Same Christmas. Different calendar." She started unpacking the ornaments, glass birds her great-grandfather had carried through two borders, and handed one to Ayah, who hung it as carefully as if she'd been told its history.

The weird part, Katherine thought while she worked, was that both of them were making the same mistake from opposite directions. Asher's mistake was simple: December 25 as a universal, a heuristic that worked fine everywhere he'd ever been, until tonight. Her mistake had been subtler and in its own quiet way more pernicious: she'd spent years treating the two dates as hers and theirs, as if her family's Christmas were a private quirk to be mentioned as little as possible. But the calendar wasn't a quirk. It was a whole other way of keeping time, and whole countries kept it, and tonight the hall was full of people for whom this was simply when Christmas came.

The priest arrived and began setting out candles. Children were pulled away from the chairs and lined up near the stage for the songs, and Katherine's mother waved her over to the tree because the top was bare and only Katherine was tall enough, even on a chair, to reach. Ayah steadied the chair legs. Asher stood with his hands still in his pockets, but he had moved closer to the tree, close enough to be handed something.

"Hold this," Katherine said, and gave him the glass bird, the blue one, the oldest. He took it in both hands.

At the stage, a boy rubbed a balloon against his sweater and held it near a strand of tinsel, and the tinsel reached toward it, every thread lifting at once as if the air around it had been ionized. The boy laughed. The priest cleared his throat. Asher lifted the bird toward the top of the tree, and Katherine, on her toes on the chair, her fingers cold against the spruce, reached down for it.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: A launch velocity v at an angle θ above the horizontal splits into a horizontal component v cos θ and a vertical component v sin θ.
story:
The garage smelled of cut grass and old paint, and Paige had claimed the workbench because the kitchen table had been claimed, hours ago, by her mother's tax papers. She spread the worksheet under the clamp light, the one her father used for soldering, and wrote her name at the top like a signature on a confession.

The problem was the third on the sheet. A ball launched at twenty meters per second at an angle of thirty degrees; find how far it travels before landing. Mr. Dhillon had drawn a little cannon on the handout, which Paige found unnecessarily cheerful, like the problem itself was malevolent but pretending to be friendly. She read it twice, then looked at the launch angle again. Thirty degrees. Barely more than a quarter of the way up from flat.

Kamryn arrived on her bike with the scrape of tires on the driveway and a paper bag of sour candies, which she set down next to Paige's calculator as tribute. "You're doing physics in a garage," Kamryn said. "In June."

"I'm doing physics in a garage in June because I failed the quiz in May." Paige pulled a second stool over with her foot. "Sit. You got the components right, I heard."

Kamryn sat, unwrapped a candy, and leaned in with the interest of someone watching a friend defuse something. Paige picked up velocity and the angle and began to split them, because that was the whole trick, she understood that much: the launch velocity v at an angle θ above the horizontal splits into a horizontal component and a vertical component, and you deal with them separately. The horizontal one does its calm, steady thing while the vertical one climbs and falls. She just couldn't remember which trig function went with which direction, and she wrote, with a small and private certainty, sine next to horizontal and cosine next to vertical.

She worked it through. The numbers came out clean, which should have been the warning. "So the vertical component," she said slowly, reading her result, "is seventeen point three meters per second. And the horizontal is ten."

Kamryn chewed her candy and said nothing, which was kind of her, because the next part Paige did to herself. She pictured the launch. Thirty degrees. A ball leaving almost flat, like a line drive, and her math was saying it would go up at seventeen meters per second while drifting sideways at ten. She looked at the cannon on the handout, so smug in its little sketch. "That ball goes almost straight up," she said. "I've mixed them up, haven't I."

"You've made a rocket," Kamryn said. "Out of a grounder."

Paige laughed, which invigorated her more than the candy would have, and crossed the numbers out. She tried it the other way, cosine for horizontal, sine for vertical, and there was a subtlety she had missed before, she realized: the angle was measured from the flat ground, so the horizontal component used the function that liked the angle itself, and the vertical one got whatever was left of the ninety degrees. She didn't have the language for it exactly, but she could feel the shape of it, the way the two pieces of the velocity traded places as the launch angle grew. At thirty degrees the ball would go sideways fast and up slowly. She redid the arithmetic and the flight time came out to about two seconds, and the range about thirty-four meters, and she sat back.

"Is that right?" she asked.

"Page two of my notes says thirty-four point something," Kamryn said. "So either we're both wrong in the same way or we're both right."

"That's the most honest thing anyone's said to me about math."

Kamryn straightened the worksheet so its edge ran parallel to the bench, an old habit, and pushed the candy bag closer to Paige's elbow. Outside, Mr. Dhillon's sprinkler came on with its ticking rotation, and the sound reached the open garage door in soft pulses. Paige copied the corrected components into her notebook in her best handwriting, the kind she saved for things she intended to keep, and beside the little cannon she drew a ball on a shallow arc, then another on a steep one, and labeled both.

"One more problem?" Kamryn asked, already sliding the sheet back toward the light.

"One more," Paige said, and picked up her pencil.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: The United States has no national sales tax; sales taxes are set by states and local governments, so the rate on a receipt depends on where the purchase is made.
story:
Elliot laid the receipts flat on the kitchen table in a fan, the way his father used to fan cards before a losing hand. Two gas-station receipts, both for the same blue raspberry slushie, both bought on Saturday during the drive to Frederick's cousin's place. One was from the stop in Hanover, one from the stop in Milford, twenty minutes down the road. Same size cup, same price before tax. Different totals.

"Are you doing a science project?" his mother asked, setting down a mug of coffee that did nothing to assuage the sour feeling in his stomach. It was Sunday night, and the tax return was spread across the other half of the table, the return his father had started in March and never finished. April was half over.

"It's math," Elliot said. "Frederick says I owe him a dollar forty."

Frederick had lent him the money at the second stop because Elliot's cash was gone, and Frederick had paid for his own slushie at both stops too, and had noticed, in the way Frederick noticed everything, that the same drink cost more in one town than the other. He had charged Elliot the difference as a debt, with interest, because Frederick intended to study business and practiced on his friends.

"Show me," his mother said, pulling a chair around beside him instead of across. She owned a hair salon and did her own returns, badly, she admitted, but she did them.

Elliot slid the receipts over. In Hanover the slushie was 2.49 plus tax and came to 2.66. In Milford it was 2.49 plus tax and came to 2.61. "Five cents," he said. "Same drink, same listed price. Frederick thinks the machine in Milford is broken, or that the Hanover clerk was skimming, some machination. He wouldn't say the word but that's what he meant. He wants his five cents plus the dollar forty he made up."

"And what do you think?"

"I think the tax is different in the two towns. Not the price. The tax." He had worked this out on the drive home, in his head, before his phone died. "There's no one national sales tax the way there's income tax. Sales tax is set by the states, and by local governments on top of that. So the rate on a receipt depends on where you buy the thing. Same chain, two towns, two rates."

His mother turned the receipts over, then back, and looked at the numbers for a while. "Your father would say that's why he does his shopping across the river," she said. "Except he never does his shopping anywhere, that's the problem." She tapped the unfinished return. "Can you look at this with me?"

Elliot pulled the folder toward him. Inside was his father's last pay stub from the landscaping company, and above it a copy of the W-2 from the same employer. He had seen his father's paycheques before, in the kitchen, but had never actually read one, and now he read the columns slowly. Gross pay, then the deductions: federal income tax, state income tax, Social Security, Medicare. The net pay at the bottom was a number he recognized as the number that came into the account every second Friday, a number he had thought of as what his father earned. It was nearly a fifth smaller than the gross.

"They take it before you get it," he said.

"That's withholding," his mother said. "The W-2 tells the government what was already taken, and the return is where you find out if they took too much or not enough." She was quiet for a second. "I think they took too much this year. I think that's why he thought we'd get money back. That's why he started it."

Elliot looked at the pay stub again, then at the receipts, then at the return with its empty lines. Two systems, one that took a share of what you earned before you ever held it, and one that added on at the register, changing its size from town to town. He had spent his bus money on a hedonistic slushie, borrowed from Frederick at a fictional interest rate, and discovered a country that taxed a drink differently depending on which side of a county line you drank it. He wasn't sure yet which system he thought was fairer, or whether fair was even the right question for either.

"Frederick still gets his five cents," his mother said. "And you can tell him the Milford machine wasn't broken. Tell him the town of Milford charges less than the town of Hanover, and he can take it up with the town of Milford."

"He'll say the town owes him a rebate."

"He'd be in good company." She handed him a pen and slid the return between them. "Line by line. You read, I'll write."

Elliot picked up the phone and texted Frederick first, typing quickly so the debt would not grow: the machines are fine, the towns tax differently, your five cents is real and coming Monday. Then he set the phone face down next to the receipts and pulled the first page of the return toward the lamplight. "Okay," he said. "Line one."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In the CDC's 2021 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, about 1 in 12 US high school students who had dated reported experiencing physical dating violence.
story:
Camille got to the coffee shop eleven minutes early, which she told herself was about getting the good table by the window, though really it was about deciding whether to stay. She ordered a lavender latte she didn't especially want, because the first time she'd said her actual order out loud, Derek had laughed and called it the most boring drink in existence, and she had been practicing, since then, being a person who ordered interesting things.

He was twenty minutes late. She spent them remembering Thursday, in the parking lot after the game, when he had taken her arm to steer her toward his friends and left marks she'd found later, four small ovals like fingerprint shadows. She had a whole vocabulary for explaining it away. He was excited. He forgot his own strength. She'd been walking the wrong direction. Each explanation was auxiliary to the main one, which was that she liked him, and she deployed them in rotation the way you rotate tires, evenly, so no single one wore out.

Alicia had seen it. That was the complication. Alicia, who worked the register here on weekends and was sliding a cloth along the counter in long, deliberate strokes, had watched Derek's hand close on Camille's arm from fifteen feet away, and Alicia did not have a rotating vocabulary. Alicia had once told their whole bio class, unprompted, that Camille's freshman boyfriend was a nightmare. She'd been right, which was the annoying thing.

He arrived at last, dropped his keys on the table, and kissed her cheek like an apology he didn't feel the need to make. "You got the window," he said. "Good. I hate being in the middle of things."

"Me too," Camille said, though she had chosen the window because she liked watching the crosswalk, the ordinary tide of people with nowhere particular to be. She caught Alicia watching her watch them and turned back to the menu she'd already ordered from.

It was in the middle of his story about the coach benching him, a story she'd heard twice, that she found herself doing the math she'd been avoiding. Ms. Zhao had put it on a slide last spring, during the unit most people slept through: in the CDC's 2021 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, about 1 in 12 US high school students who had dated reported experiencing physical dating violence. Camille had written it in her notebook because she liked the sound of "epidemiology," the idea that heartbreak could be counted, tabulated, mapped like weather. One in twelve. Thirty kids in her grade had dated someone that year, by her rough count, which meant two or three of them, walking the halls with fingerprint shadows, and she had always pictured some other girl, some girl who wasn't practicing being interesting for anyone.

She wasn't sure, though, and she let herself be unsure. Grabbing an arm once was not the same as what the survey counted; the survey said physical dating violence, and she didn't know exactly where the line fell, whether a line could even be drawn by a number. Derek was telling her about his plan to monetize his highlight videos, a word he used like a spell, and under the table her thumb found the ovals on her arm and pressed one, lightly, testing whether it was hers.

Alicia came over with a water refill Camille hadn't asked for and didn't move away. "Ms. Zhao still doing that health unit?" she said, to no one in particular, wiping the table's corner. "The survey stuff. One in twelve kids who dated. Somebody should put that on a poster in the gym instead of the diet ones." She straightened, looked at Derek with a pleasant, level face, and said, "Refills are for customers who order boring drinks. House rule."

"That's not a rule," Derek said.

"It's my rule," Alicia said, and went back to the counter.

Derek laughed, a short sound with a hinge on it. "Your friend's a lot."

Camille looked at the crosswalk, where the light had changed and a man in an aux cord tangle of headphone wire waited for nothing, having missed his moment. She thought, briefly and without ceremony, that she had also missed a moment, several of them, and that there would be more, and that some of them she would take and some she would stand beside with her hands in her lap. Then she picked up her interesting drink, which had gone cold, and drank it anyway.

"I think I'm going to head out," she said. "You can text me if you want." She said it as a question and an answer at once, and left it there on the table beside his keys, not waiting to see which one he'd hear. Outside, the light changed again, and Alicia was already at the door, untying her apron.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Most US employment is at-will, meaning the employer or the worker can end the job at any time for any reason that is not illegal.
story:
The application took eleven minutes, most of it spent inventing answers to questions about her personality. Alice wrote that she was dependable, then crossed it out and wrote punctual, which at least was checkable. The store was the one three blocks from her house, the one where she'd bought popsicles her whole childhood, and when the manager called her in for an interview he mostly talked about how hard it was to find people who showed up. He hired her before she'd finished her water. She walked home with the schedule in her back pocket, feeling the paper's edge through her jeans all the way to the door.

Her mother said it was good to have a job, and then, in the same breath, that she should focus on grades, and that senior spring was for making memories. Alice took this to mean that her mother wanted both things and would judge her for whichever one slipped. She said she could handle Sundays and two evenings. She did not mention that the evenings were the ones Caylee and Steve had started reserving for the quarry, where the water was still too cold but everyone went anyway.

Training consisted of a laminated sheet about produce codes and a woman named Ms. Menon, who had worked register nine for longer than the store had been called by its current name, showing her how to angle the barcode so it read on the first pass. Ms. Menon had a way of moving through the eight-hour shift that made it look like nothing, hands arriving where they were needed a half-second early. Alice watched her and thought of the word ductile, from chemistry class, a metal that bends without breaking, and thought that Ms. Menon had been bent a very long time.

By the third week she had learned the following: that closing meant mopping under the registers where coins had fused to something syrupy, that customers forgave almost anything except a slow line, and that the assistant manager, whose name she deliberately kept forgetting, believed new hires existed to be tested. He sent her to the back for a price check on an item with no price, twice. He watched her count her drawer like she might pocket a five. Caylee, when Alice complained, laughed and said, "So quit. You don't even have to give notice. Most jobs here are at-will, meaning they can fire you or you can quit any time, for any reason that's not illegal." Steve, who was between jobs himself, nodded along like this was old news to him.

Alice went home and ruminated on it, turning the phrase over while she should have been outlining a paper. At-will. It had a clean sound, like something a lawyer would keep in a drawer. She understood that it cut both ways, and she understood something else that took longer to surface: that the same rule that let her walk out at the end of a shift let them let her go at the end of one too, and that the assistant manager probably knew it as well as she did. Freedom, if that was the word, seemed to run in the same channel as the insecurity. She couldn't figure out whether she'd been handed a door or a warning, and she suspected the honest answer was that the door and the warning were the same object, seen from different sides.

The test came sooner than she expected. On a Thursday the assistant manager told her the Sunday shifts were being reassigned, effective immediately, no reason offered, and she stood there realizing that none was required. When she asked about the schedule for June, he said June would sort itself out, in a tone that suggested it would sort itself out without her. That night she lay awake doing the arithmetic of a job she'd had for a month and might lose in a week, and of the gas money she'd already promised to her mother, and of the fact that quitting before being let go would look, in some ledger she couldn't see, like the same thing.

She went back Friday unsure what she intended to do, which was perhaps why she did what she did. The assistant manager was on register two, arguing with a customer about an expired coupon, and Alice could see the moment building toward a scene, the line tightening behind them. Ms. Menon caught her eye from nine and tipped her head almost imperceptibly. Alice opened register four, called "I can help whoever's next," and took the line, and for forty minutes the store ran and nobody yelled. When it was over the assistant manager said nothing at all, which she understood was his version of losing.

She didn't quit that night, and she didn't get the Sundays back either. What she decided, walking the long way home with her check in her pocket, was smaller and harder to say out loud: that she would stay as long as it was worth it and leave when it wasn't, on a day she chose, and that this was a right she hadn't earned so much as been handed along with everyone else, and that it protected almost nothing except her ability to walk. She had wanted the job to be a sinecure, some small undemanding pocket of money, and instead it was a place where she'd learned to work and a place that could end her on a Tuesday, and both of those turned out to be true at once, neither canceling the other.

At the quarry that weekend the water had finally warmed. Caylee asked from the rock ledge whether Alice was still at the store, and Alice said she was, for now. Then she pulled her shirt over her head, ran the wet stones, and jumped.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: The phrase 'rule of thirds' was first written down by John Thomas Smith in his 1797 book Remarks on Rural Scenery.
story:
The smell at the community studio on Saturdays was linseed oil and burnt coffee, and Jordyn had come to think of it as the smell of permission. She had a scholarship portfolio due in eleven days, and one painting left, a landscape of the creek behind her grandmother's house. She stood at her easel now with the horizon line sketched dead center, and it looked, she thought, like a painting hanging in a dentist's office.

Kianna leaned over from the next easel, brush between her teeth, and pointed at the canvas. "Put the horizon a third of the way down," she said around the brush. "It's the rule of thirds. Instantly better."

"Who made that a rule?" Jordyn said.

"Some dead guy, probably." Kianna went back to her portrait of her little brother, who was sulking in the corner with a juice box. "Painters just know stuff like that. Ask Alvin, he reads."

Alvin was at the long table by the window, doing something elaborate with a wire sculpture and a pair of pliers. He did read, that was true, but he also liked being asked, which Jordyn sometimes found exhausting and sometimes found useful. "Actually," he said, not looking up, "I know that one. It was first written down by John Thomas Smith in his 1797 book, Remarks on Rural Scenery. I found it when I was researching an essay on landscape engraving."

"The whole rule?" Jordyn said. "One guy?"

"One guy, one book. Before that, painters were doing it without calling it anything."

Jordyn looked at her canvas again. The creek, the willow, the flat gray Ohio sky her grandmother used to call the sky's clemency, as if the weather were a judge deciding not to punish anyone. A horizon a third of the way down would leave two thirds of sky, and the sky over that creek was most of what she remembered, the way it went on and on over nothing.

She moved the line. She repainted the water lower, let the sky open up, and it did look better, immediately, undeniably better, and she hated that it was that easy. She had wanted the painting to be hers through struggle, through some process that would transmute her eleven years of Saturday afternoons into something a scholarship committee would recognize as talent. Instead she had taken a tip from a dead engraver she'd never heard of.

Ms. Leblanc, who ran the studio and mostly fixed kilns and ordered gesso, came by with her mug of burnt coffee. She looked at the canvas for a long moment. "Better," she said. "The sky's doing work now."

"It's the rule of thirds," Jordyn said, and heard herself sound slightly doctrinaire, like a student reciting, and heard Kianna snort at the next easel. "It was written down by a guy named John Thomas Smith, in 1797. Some book about rural scenery."

"Remarks on Rural Scenery," Alvin called from the window, faithful to detail even at a distance.

"Fine," Ms. Leblanc said. "But Smith wrote down what eyes already liked. He didn't invent the liking." She sipped her coffee and looked at the canvas again. "Question is whether the liking is yours."

Jordyn worked through the afternoon on that question. She tried the horizon back in the center, low and stubborn, and it looked like a dentist's office again, and she tried it a third of the way down and it looked right, and neither experiment told her whether right meant true. She kept the lower horizon. She painted the willow leaning left, into all that sky, and gave the water a broken reflection of it, so the tree existed twice. Somewhere in there the painting stopped feeling like Smith's idea. The rule had given her the room, and what she put in the room was her grandmother's creek, the milk crates on the bank, the one lawn chair with its seat gone.

At five o'clock Kianna packed up her brother and his juice box, and Alvin carried his wire sculpture out with the tenderness of someone transporting a sleeping animal. Ms. Leblanc locked the supply cabinet and stood beside Jordyn, who was still there, still looking.

"It's good," Ms. Leblanc said. "It's honest, anyway."

"I don't know if I believe in the rule," Jordyn said. "I believe in the painting."

"That's allowed," Ms. Leblanc said. She rinsed her mug in the utility sink, and the water ran gray for a second before it ran clear. "Lock up when you're done."

Jordyn stayed another ten minutes. Then she pulled the canvas off the easel, carried it to the rack by the door where the finished work waited for Monday, and set it in the slot with her name taped to the edge, the willow doubled in the water, the sky taking up its two thirds, the horizon exactly where a dead man had told her to put it, and the lawn chair, slightly off from everything, where she had wanted it.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A metronome marking of 60 means sixty beats per minute, exactly one beat per second.
story:
Colton had been slicing the fast run in the third movement into wreckage for two weeks, and Mr. Suzuki had finally stopped letting him get away with it. The studio smelled of rosin and old radiator dust, and the metronome sat on the piano lid like a small wooden pyramid that had opinions. "Again," Mr. Suzuki said, and Colton raised the bow, and again the sixteenth notes collided somewhere in the middle like cars in an intersection where everyone had decided the light was merely advisory.

"You are faster than the music," Mr. Suzuki said. He was not effusive with praise, which Colton had learned to prefer, because when he did say something warm it meant something. "Faster than your own hands. So we will make time itself slower." He reached over and turned the dial on the metronome all the way down until the arm swung in a wide, unhurried arc, tick, tick, tick, and the brass plate read 60.

Colton stared at it. Tick. He counted under his breath, one, tick, two, tick, and something assembled itself in his mind without anyone building it for him. He looked at the second hand of the clock above the piano and watched it sweep a full circle. The tick and the second hand arrived together, over and over, sixty times. "It's the same as a second," he said. "Sixty, that's exactly one beat per second. Sixty beats in a minute." Mr. Suzuki only nodded, the way he nodded when a student had done the discovering himself.

At that speed the run was almost embarrassing. One note per tick, whole seconds of air between them, the phrase stripped of everything that had made it exhilarate him when he first heard the recording, the momentum, the sprint, the applause-earning cascade. It felt like reciting a phone number. He said so, and Mr. Suzuki tilted his head. "Yes. For now it is a phone number. Learn the number, then learn to say it like a sentence."

Raquel would have laughed at him, he knew. She had come over on Tuesday to work on their history presentation and found him practicing the passage at the glacial tempo, and she had sat on his bed making slow-motion explosion noises until he threw a pillow at her. But he'd noticed something then, and he noticed it again now: at one beat per second there was room to notice things. That his second finger was landing late on the B flat every single time, a habit he'd been deaf to at speed. That he was gripping the bow like it owed him money. At full tempo the errors hid inside each other. Slowed down, they stood apart, embarrassed, available.

He had assumed, before, that the point of practicing was to sound good, and the point of sounding good was the moment at the winter recital when the fast movement would land and the room would go quiet in that specific way. That was one way to think about it. But Mr. Suzuki seemed to think the point was the slow part, the unglamorous part, the part nobody would ever hear. Colton wasn't sure these two ideas were the same thing, or even friends. He only knew that the phone number was turning into a sentence, and that when he bumped the dial up to 80 and then 100 across the week, the B flat came down on time, and his hand didn't tighten, because his hand had learned where the notes lived when there had been whole seconds to find them.

The night before the recital he set the metronome back to 60 one more time, just to check. He played the run at one beat per second, the long silences between the notes full of nothing but the tick and his own careful breath, and it occurred to him that this was the truest version he had, the version with all the lights on. The fast version was the same notes in the dark.

At the recital he sat in the folding chair behind the curtain with his heart going hard, and Raquel leaned over from the row behind him, where she had shown up even though she'd claimed the whole thing was an affectation, rich kids performing effort for each other. "Break a string," she whispered, which was her language for good luck. The curtain opened. He walked out, set the music, raised the bow, and before the accompanist came in he tapped his foot once against the stage, quietly, marking a second.
